title: Data Vault Hub Design for Multi-Source Customer IDs
scenario_context: A retail enterprise ingests customer records from three source systems: a legacy CRM (customer IDs like CRM-00123), a mobile app (UUIDs), and a third-party loyalty program (integer member IDs). The data engineering team is building a Data Vault on Snowflake. One engineer proposes a single Customer Hub with a composite business key (source_system + source_id). Another proposes one Hub per source system, linked via a same-as Link. The systems have no guaranteed cross-system identifier: roughly 30% of customers appear in two or more systems, identified only by fuzzy email matching. The architecture must support onboarding additional customer source systems in the future without modifying existing hub keys or satellite structures. Identity resolution artifacts must be first-class raw vault constructs — fully auditable and reprocessable against the raw vault independently of any downstream mart — not delegated to information mart transformations.
description: Which Data Vault hub design correctly handles the multi-source customer identity problem while preserving raw source fidelity and allowing identity resolution to evolve independently?
options: Option A — One Hub per source system (CRM Hub, App Hub, Loyalty Hub), connected through a same-as Link (Identity Link). Fuzzy email matching populates the Link and can be updated as matching rules evolve without altering Hub records.

Option B — A single Customer Hub with a composite business key of (source_system, source_id). One Hub row per source record; identity resolution is deferred to the information mart layer via a bridge table.
Option C — A single Customer Hub keyed on a golden-record email address produced by a matching engine upstream of the vault. All source IDs map to the email-based Hub hashkey.

Option D — One Hub per source system, but identity resolution is enforced as a referential integrity constraint on the same-as Link so that every Hub row must resolve to exactly one golden identity before loading is allowed.
explanation:
Option A is correct. Data Vault's core principle is to load raw source keys without transformation. One Hub per source system keeps business keys pure and un-merged. A same-as (or identity) Link explicitly models the uncertain, evolving relationship between source entities — because matching rules change, the Link rows can be reloaded or corrected without touching Hubs or Satellites. This separates ingestion concerns from identity resolution concerns.

Option B is a common mistake: a composite (source_system + source_id) key in a single Hub technically works but conflates multiple business domains into one Hub, complicating Satellite attachment and making it harder to evolve individual source feeds. Data Vault best practice is one Hub per business concept per source when keys are not interoperable.

Option C is the most dangerous distractor. Applying upstream matching to derive a golden email before vaulting violates the raw-source-fidelity principle — the vault no longer represents what the source actually provided, and if the matching logic is wrong you cannot reconstruct the original records. The vault should preserve facts as received; identity resolution belongs in the business vault or information mart.

Option D adds a RI constraint that defeats the purpose of the same-as Link. The entire point is to allow uncertain, asynchronous resolution. Blocking loads until every record resolves to a golden identity reintroduces the coupling that Data Vault is designed to eliminate and will cause load failures whenever matching is incomplete.
hints: Consider which layer of the architecture is responsible for identity resolution versus raw ingestion — they should not be the same.
Consider what happens when a fourth source system is onboarded later: how does each design handle the addition without touching existing hub structures or requiring satellite re-attachment?

What happens to your ingestion pipeline if the entity-matching rules turn out to be wrong and you need to reprocess them? Which architectural layer should absorb that reprocessing cost — the raw ingestion layer or a separate resolution layer?

title: Choosing the Right SCD Strategy for Analyst-Facing Price History
scenario_context: An analytics team at an online marketplace maintains a product dimension that tracks the listed price of each product. Business analysts need to: (1) see the price that was in effect at the time of each historical order (point-in-time accuracy), (2) quickly query 'what is the current price?' without filtering on date ranges, and (3) occasionally run reports comparing last month's prices against a stable, slowly evolving 'reference price' that rolls up infrequently. The dimension has roughly 4 million products and prices change at an average rate of 2% of the catalog per day.
description: Which slowly changing dimension strategy best satisfies all three analyst requirements given the scale and update rate?
options: Option A — SCD Type 6 (hybrid): maintain current_price as a physical column on all rows (updated on each change), valid_from/valid_to date range columns for history, and a separate is_current flag. Queries for current price use the flag; historical joins use date ranges.

Option B — SCD Type 2 only: add a new row on each price change with valid_from/valid_to. Current price queries use WHERE is_current = true. Reference price is computed in a downstream dbt model by taking the last row per product per month.

Option C — SCD Type 1 only: overwrite price on change. Build a separate price_history table as an append-only log using dbt snapshots. Reference price is the current product row; historical accuracy comes from the snapshot log joined at query time.

Option D — SCD Type 4: maintain the current-state product dimension as a Type 1 table, and offload full history to a separate mini-dimension or history table. Analysts join the mini-dimension for point-in-time queries and the base table for current-price queries.
explanation:
Option A (SCD Type 6) is the best fit because it satisfies all three requirements without a query-time join or secondary table: the current_price column answers requirement 2 without a date-range filter scan, valid_from/valid_to rows answer requirement 1 for point-in-time joins, and the stable current_price column (updated in-place across all historical rows) can serve as the 'reference price' column if desired. The tradeoff is storage (4M products × average row count per product), but at 2% daily churn the history depth is manageable.

Option B (Type 2 only) satisfies requirements 1 and 2 but not 3 elegantly. There is no built-in 'reference price' concept; computing it from the last row per product per month in a downstream dbt model adds query complexity and can drift if the cadence is inconsistent. Type 2 alone is insufficient when analysts also need a stable current-price column that doesn't require date filtering.

Option C (Type 1 + snapshot log) sacrifices point-in-time accuracy in the main dimension. Analysts querying the base table get only the current value; joining the snapshot log at query time is expensive at 4M-product scale and puts burden on every consumer. This is a common pattern but fails the 'historical orders at correct price' requirement without significant join overhead.

Option D (Type 4) is a legitimate pattern but introduces a second table that every historical query must join. At 4M products with a 2% daily update rate, the mini-dimension grows rapidly and still requires date-range logic. Type 4 is most appropriate when the changing attributes are so frequently queried separately that partitioning into a mini-dimension reduces scan cost — not the case here, where all three requirements center on the same price attribute.
hints: All three requirements (historical accuracy, current-price lookup, stable reference) can potentially be satisfied by a single design — consider which versioning strategy physically maintains a full row for every change while also making the current value accessible without date-range filtering.
Type 2 satisfies historical accuracy but imposes a date-range filter on every current-price query. Consider which hybrid approach adds a column that eliminates that filter cost.
SCD Type 6 carries the current value forward on all rows AND preserves full history with date ranges — evaluate it against each of the three stated requirements explicitly.

title: Grain Definition for Accumulating Snapshot Fact Tables
scenario_context: A logistics company tracks the lifecycle of each shipment through five milestones: order_placed, picked_up, in_transit, out_for_delivery, and delivered. A data analyst asks for a fact table that lets them compute the time elapsed between each milestone and identify which step causes the most delay. Some shipments skip the out_for_delivery milestone (bulk B2B drops). The proposed design has one row per shipment, with five date columns and five corresponding lag_hours columns. A data engineer argues the grain should instead be one row per shipment per milestone event, making it a transaction fact table.
description: Which grain and table design is most appropriate for a pipeline-stage delay analysis workload?
options: Option A — One row per shipment (accumulating snapshot). Each milestone is a separate date column; lag_hours columns are derived. NULL milestone columns represent skipped stages. This grain is purpose-built for elapsed-time queries across a fixed pipeline.

Option B — One row per shipment per milestone event (transaction fact table). Elapsed time between steps is computed at query time using window functions. Skipped milestones simply have no row, avoiding NULLs entirely.

Option C — Two fact tables: an accumulating snapshot for completed shipments (all milestones filled) and a transaction fact for in-flight shipments. Analysts query the snapshot for delay analysis and the transaction table for real-time status.

Option D — One row per shipment with milestone timestamps stored as a JSON array column. Elapsed-time logic is pushed into a dbt macro that unnests the array. This avoids schema changes when new milestones are added.
explanation:
Option A is correct. The accumulating snapshot fact table is precisely designed for pipeline-stage workflows where a single entity (the shipment) moves through a known sequence of milestones. Each row represents the full lifecycle of one shipment. Elapsed-time calculations between stages are simple column subtractions — no window functions, no self-joins. NULL milestone columns for skipped stages (B2B out_for_delivery) are expected and semantically meaningful in this pattern. The grain 'one row per shipment' is correct because the unit of analysis is the shipment's complete journey.

Option B (transaction fact) is the most tempting distractor. It avoids NULLs and handles variable milestone sequences well. However, elapsed-time queries require window functions (LAG or self-join on shipment_id ordered by event_time), which are significantly more complex and potentially expensive at scale. For a delay-analysis workload where the pipeline is well-defined, this complexity is unnecessary overhead. Transaction facts are better suited for workloads where you need arbitrary aggregations by event type rather than inter-stage elapsed time.

Option C sounds like a pragmatic compromise, but it creates a synchronization problem: shipments transition from 'in-flight' to 'completed' at delivery, requiring logic to move rows between tables. This dual-table approach also means analysts must union or switch between tables for end-to-end delay analysis, complicating the query layer unnecessarily.

Option D (JSON array) is an anti-pattern in a structured analytical warehouse. Storing milestone timestamps in a JSON column sacrifices columnar compression, predicate pushdown, and type safety. It also makes schema changes harder to govern, not easier — downstream models that unnest the JSON must be updated when milestone definitions change. This trades schema clarity for false flexibility.
hints: Consider which table design makes elapsed-time queries between stages as simple as column subtraction versus requiring window functions or self-joins.
The accumulating snapshot pattern is specifically designed for workflows with a defined sequence of milestones for a single entity — evaluate whether a shipment lifecycle fits this description.
NULL milestone columns in an accumulating snapshot are semantically meaningful (milestone not reached or skipped), not a design defect.

title: Wide OBT vs. Normalized Model for ML Feature Generation
scenario_context: A data science team at a fintech company needs a feature store input table for a credit risk model. The table must join customer demographics, account balance history (daily snapshots for 365 days), transaction aggregates (30/60/90-day windows), and bureau credit score history (monthly updates). The ML platform expects a single wide table per customer per scoring date. The data engineering team debates between (a) building one wide One-Big-Table (OBT) with all features pre-joined and pre-aggregated, materialized daily as a full refresh, and (b) maintaining normalized intermediate models (one per feature family) joined in a final mart view. The scoring table has approximately 2 million customers and is scored daily.
description: Which modeling approach is most appropriate for this ML feature generation workload, and why?
options: Option A — Normalized intermediate models (one per feature family) materialized as tables, with a final wide mart built as a SELECT * from each, joined on customer_id and scoring_date. The mart is incremental on scoring_date. Recomputing a single feature family does not require rebuilding the full wide table.

Option B — A single OBT materialized as a full daily refresh. All feature logic lives in one model, making lineage simple and ensuring consistent snapshot semantics across all feature families for a given scoring date.

Option C — A single OBT with incremental materialization using scoring_date as the incremental key. New scoring dates append rows; existing dates are never updated, avoiding full-refresh cost at 2M customers × 365 days.

Option D — Normalized intermediate models built as views (not materialized tables). The final mart is also a view. Compute is deferred to query time, saving storage and ensuring all feature logic is always evaluated on the latest source data.
explanation:
Option A is correct. Normalized intermediate models materialized as tables (one per feature family) provide the right balance of modularity and performance. When a feature family's logic changes or a backfill is needed, only that family's model is recomputed — not the entire wide table. The final wide mart as an incremental model on scoring_date means only today's scoring rows are computed on each daily run. This is critical at 2M customers: a full refresh of the wide table would be expensive and slow, while incremental on the family tables keeps each family's backfill targeted.

Option B (single OBT full refresh) is simple for lineage but operationally costly. A full refresh of 2M customer × wide-feature rows daily means recomputing all feature logic from source on every run. If any one feature family's source data is delayed, the entire table is stale. Debugging a feature regression means inspecting a monolithic model instead of an isolated family model.

Option C improves on B by making the OBT incremental, but concentrating all feature logic in one model creates a single point of failure. An incremental OBT with a scoring_date key works only if feature logic is stable; backfilling any feature means either a full refresh (defeating the purpose) or complex conditional logic to recompute historical rows. More importantly, a scoring_date-keyed incremental model assumes features are never recomputed for past dates — which breaks for late-arriving bureau data.

Option D (all views) avoids storage cost but creates a query-time compute explosion. A 2M-row wide table with 365-day balance history unnested at query time would be prohibitively slow for an ML platform that must run feature generation as a nightly batch. Deferring compute to query time is appropriate for low-volume analytical exploration, not nightly ML batch ingestion.
hints: Consider what happens when a single feature family's source data is delayed or its logic needs to change — which design isolates that impact?
Incremental materialization on a wide OBT creates a backfill problem if any feature's logic changes — think about which design allows targeted recomputation per feature family.
Materialized intermediate tables per feature family allow each to be independently versioned, backfilled, and tested before being joined into the final wide mart.

title: Pre-Aggregation vs. Live Query for High-Cardinality Dashboard
scenario_context: An e-commerce company's executive dashboard shows daily, weekly, and monthly revenue by region, product category, and customer segment. The underlying orders table has 800 million rows and grows by ~5 million rows per day. The BI tool issues ad-hoc GROUP BY queries directly against the warehouse. P95 dashboard load time is 45 seconds — unacceptably slow. The data team considers three options: (a) pre-aggregate to a daily_revenue_summary table refreshed nightly, (b) create a materialized view that refreshes incrementally on each warehouse load, or (c) add clustering keys on (order_date, region, product_category) to the base table and tune query patterns.
description: Which approach best reduces dashboard latency while preserving query flexibility for ad-hoc slicing at the region/category/segment level?
options: Option A — Pre-aggregate to a daily_revenue_summary table at the (date, region, category, segment) grain, refreshed nightly. Dashboard queries hit the summary table; ad-hoc slicing remains flexible across all four dimensions because the grain is already fully crossed.

Option B — Materialized view on the base table refreshed incrementally after each load. The MV pre-joins and groups to (date, region, category), but excludes segment to keep refresh cost low. Segment slicing requires a live query on the MV output joined back to the base table.

Option C — Add clustering on (order_date, region, product_category) to the base table and push a query result cache at the BI layer. No pre-aggregation; dashboard loads from cache after first hit and queries prune partitions efficiently.

Option D — Build a separate OLAP cube (e.g., Redshift AQUA or BigQuery BI Engine) sitting in front of the warehouse. All dashboard traffic hits the cube; the warehouse is used only for ad-hoc deep queries.
explanation:
Option A is correct. Pre-aggregating to a daily_revenue_summary table at the fully crossed grain (date × region × category × segment) dramatically reduces query scan cost — the summary table has at most date_count × region_count × category_count × segment_count rows, which is orders of magnitude fewer than 800M rows. Because all four slicing dimensions are included in the grain, the dashboard can filter and re-aggregate across any combination without touching the base table. Nightly refresh means the summary is always 24 hours stale, which is acceptable for an executive dashboard showing daily/weekly/monthly metrics.

Option B avoids the full grain crossing by excluding segment, which reduces the MV's refresh cost but breaks the query flexibility requirement. Segment slicing now requires joining the MV back to the base table, defeating the purpose of pre-aggregation and reintroducing 800M-row scans for segment-sliced views.

Option C (clustering + cache) is the lowest-effort option and can meaningfully reduce scan cost via partition pruning, but clustering alone on an 800M-row table still results in multi-second scans when queries aren't perfectly selective. A BI cache helps for repeated identical queries but fails for ad-hoc exploration. This approach doesn't fundamentally solve the problem at scale — it defers it.

Option D (OLAP cube) solves the problem but introduces significant operational overhead: a separate system to maintain, sync, and monitor. OLAP cubes are appropriate when dimension cardinality is very high and query patterns are known and fixed. For a four-dimensional summary at this cardinality, a pre-aggregated summary table in the warehouse achieves the same result without the architectural complexity.
hints: Consider what the minimum unit of analysis is that satisfies all four slicing dimensions the dashboard requires — then evaluate whether any option omits a dimension from pre-aggregation.
A pre-aggregated table at the fully crossed grain of all dashboard dimensions can serve all dashboard queries without touching the base fact table, regardless of which dimension is filtered.

The tradeoff between a materialized view (incremental refresh, partial grain) and a nightly summary table (full refresh, full grain) turns on whether excluding segment from the MV creates a query path back to the base table.

title: Data Vault Satellite Design for Multi-Source Attribute Conflicts
scenario_context: A financial services firm loads customer contact attributes (name, address, phone, email) from two source systems: a core banking system (CBS) and a KYC vendor API. Both systems provide the same attributes for the same customer (resolved via a same-as Link). CBS data is updated nightly; KYC data arrives weekly. Analysts must be able to query: (a) the most recent value from each source independently, (b) which source was authoritative at any point in time, and (c) historical changes from either source. A junior engineer proposes merging both sources into a single Customer Satellite with a 'source_system' discriminator column.
description: What is the correct Data Vault satellite design for multi-source attributes that conflict between sources?
options: Option A — One Satellite per source system (CBS_Customer_Satellite and KYC_Customer_Satellite), each with its own load_date and record_source. The same-as Link connects the two Hub rows. Source-specific history and cross-source comparison are both preserved without merging.

Option B — A single multi-source Satellite with a composite primary key of (hub_hashkey, load_date, source_system). Queries filter on source_system to get per-source history; conflict resolution logic is pushed to the information mart.

Option C — A single Satellite with a 'golden record' merge rule applied upstream: the KYC vendor's values overwrite CBS values when both are non-null. Load_date tracks when the merged record was last updated.

Option D — One Satellite per attribute family: a name_satellite, address_satellite, and contact_satellite — each with load_date and record_source. This allows individual attribute staleness to be tracked independently of other attributes.
explanation:
Option A is correct. Data Vault's Satellite design principle is one Satellite per source system (or per rate-of-change group, when multiple sources feed the same Hub). Separate Satellites for CBS and KYC preserve raw source fidelity, maintain independent load histories, and allow the same-as Link to model the relationship between the two Hub entities. Analysts can query each Satellite independently for source-specific history or join both to compare values at any point in time. The conflict resolution logic — which source wins for a given use case — is deliberately pushed to the information mart layer, not embedded in the vault.

Option B is a tempting pragmatic shortcut. Adding a source_system discriminator column to a single Satellite works mechanically but creates a composite primary key that doesn't align with standard Data Vault patterns. More importantly, it conflates two sources' histories into a single structure, making it harder to independently evolve or reprocess one source's feed. It also loses the clean separation of concerns that separate Satellites provide.

Option C (upstream merge/golden record) violates Data Vault's most fundamental rule: never transform or merge source data before loading it into the vault. Applying override rules upstream means the vault no longer reflects what either source actually provided. If the merge rule is wrong, there is no way to reconstruct either source's original values from the vault alone.

Option D (one Satellite per attribute) is a legitimate Data Vault pattern when attributes have significantly different rates of change (e.g., address changes weekly; name changes yearly). However, for this scenario, the primary distinction is by source system, not by attribute. Splitting by attribute family when the source distinction is more significant adds unnecessary complexity without addressing the multi-source conflict problem.
hints: Think about which dimension of variation (source system vs. attribute type vs. change frequency) should drive Satellite splitting in a case with two distinct source systems.
The 'one Satellite per source system' rule ensures raw source fidelity and independent load histories — evaluate which options violate this by merging sources before loading.
In Data Vault, conflict resolution between sources belongs in the information mart layer, not in the raw vault or business vault loading logic.

title: Referential Integrity Constraints in a Cloud Analytical Warehouse
scenario_context: A data team is designing a dimensional model in Snowflake for a retail analytics platform. The model has a central sales fact table (300M rows/month) joined to five dimensions: customer, product, store, date, and promotion. The team debates whether to enforce referential integrity (RI) constraints (foreign keys) on the fact table. In Snowflake, foreign keys are informational only — they are never enforced at write time. An advocate for RI argues that declaring constraints improves query plan optimization. An opponent argues that unenforced constraints on dirty ETL data create false confidence and that data quality should be enforced in dbt tests instead.
description: What is the correct approach to referential integrity in an analytical warehouse like Snowflake, given the tradeoffs between optimizer hints, data quality assurance, and ETL realities?
options: Option A — Declare foreign key constraints as informational metadata (Snowflake will not enforce them), AND run dbt relationship tests on every ETL load to catch orphaned fact rows before they enter the warehouse. The two mechanisms serve different purposes: RI metadata aids the optimizer; dbt tests enforce data quality.

Option B — Do not declare RI constraints in Snowflake because they are unenforced and give false confidence. Rely solely on dbt relationship tests. Declaring phantom constraints introduces risk if a future engineer assumes they are enforced.

Option C — Enforce referential integrity by adding a pre-load deduplication and orphan-drop step in the ETL pipeline that removes fact rows with no matching dimension key. This ensures RI is always satisfied without relying on database constraints or dbt tests.

Option D — Use Snowflake's UNIQUE and NOT NULL constraints (which are enforced) instead of foreign keys. Define surrogate key uniqueness on all dimension tables and NOT NULL on fact dimension key columns. This provides partial RI enforcement that the engine actually guarantees.
explanation:
Option A is correct. In Snowflake (and most cloud analytical warehouses like BigQuery and Redshift), foreign key constraints are declared but not enforced at write time. However, the optimizer CAN use them as hints for join elimination and query plan optimization — particularly for star schema queries where a dimension filter implies a fact table filter. Declaring them as metadata is therefore not worthless. Separately, dbt relationship tests (or equivalent pipeline quality checks) provide the actual data quality gate before data enters the warehouse. The two mechanisms are complementary: metadata for optimizer hints, tests for correctness guarantees.

Option B is the most common expert-level mistake. Refusing to declare RI metadata because it's unenforced sacrifices the optimizer hint benefit. Modern Snowflake documentation explicitly recommends declaring constraints for query optimization even though they're not enforced. The 'false confidence' risk is real but manageable through team documentation and tooling, not by removing potentially useful metadata.

Option C (pre-load orphan drop) enforces data quality by silently deleting business data. Dropping fact rows with missing dimension keys can mask ETL problems and lead to revenue undercounting or audit failures. The correct response to orphaned rows is to investigate and fix the upstream issue, not to silently remove them.

Option D conflates different constraint types. NOT NULL on fact dimension key columns is a useful and enforceable constraint — it prevents null foreign keys. But UNIQUE on dimension surrogate keys doesn't constitute RI; it only ensures the dimension has no duplicate keys. The foreign key relationship (fact rows must have matching dimension rows) is still unenforced. This option provides a false sense of having addressed RI.
hints: In cloud analytical warehouses, foreign key constraints and data quality enforcement are separate concerns — consider which tools are best suited to each.
Even unenforced RI declarations can provide value to the query optimizer — look up how Snowflake uses constraint metadata before concluding they have no purpose.
Silently dropping orphaned fact rows solves a symptom rather than the cause of an ETL data quality problem — think about the downstream implications for business metric accuracy.

title: Modeling a Many-to-Many Promotion-Product Relationship in a Star Schema
scenario_context: A retail analytics team is extending their dimensional model to support promotion analysis. Each promotion can apply to multiple products, and each product can be active in multiple concurrent promotions. The promotions dimension currently has one row per promotion. Analysts need to answer: (a) which promotions are active for a given product on a given date, (b) how many products are covered by each promotion, and (c) what revenue lift is attributable to promotions by product. The sales fact table has one row per transaction line item (product_id, store_id, date_id, quantity, revenue).
description: Which modeling approach correctly handles the many-to-many relationship between promotions and products while supporting all three analytical questions?
options: Option A — Add a promotion_bridge table (product_id, promotion_id, effective_date, expiry_date, weight_factor) linking the product dimension to the promotion dimension. The sales fact table retains a single promotion_id for the 'primary' promotion; analysts join through the bridge for multi-promotion analysis.

Option B — Denormalize by adding a promotion_ids array column to the product dimension, updated via SCD Type 1 overwrites. Explode the array at query time to answer multi-promotion questions. This avoids a bridge table and keeps the star schema flat.

Option C — Redesign the sales fact to include a promotion_id foreign key column. For transactions with multiple concurrent promotions, insert multiple fact rows (one per applicable promotion) with revenue split by a weight factor. The promotion dimension remains Type 2 for history.

Option D — Create a promotion_coverage_fact table at the grain of (product_id, promotion_id, coverage_date) with a boolean is_active flag. This separates promotion coverage from transaction facts and supports all three questions independently of the sales fact table.
explanation:
Option A is correct. The bridge table pattern (or role-playing dimension bridge) is the standard dimensional modeling solution for a many-to-many relationship between a fact table dimension and a related entity. The promotion_bridge table at the (product_id, promotion_id, effective_date) grain allows analysts to: (a) filter the bridge by date to find active promotions for a product, (b) count distinct products per promotion, and (c) join the sales fact to the bridge and then to the promotion dimension for revenue lift analysis. Including a weight_factor column (e.g., 0.5 if two promotions are concurrent) enables fair revenue attribution across promotions. The sales fact retains a single primary promotion_id for the simple case, with the bridge serving multi-promotion analysis.

Option B (array column in the product dimension) is a common anti-pattern in analytical warehouses. Array columns require explode operations at query time, which can be expensive at scale and are not universally supported by all BI tools. More importantly, embedding promotion membership in the product dimension conflates two different business concepts — product attributes and promotion coverage — and makes SCD management for promotions extremely complex.

Option C (one fact row per promotion with split revenue) inflates the fact table's row count in proportion to promotion concurrency and introduces a derived revenue column. Splitting revenue by a weight factor at fact load time bakes a business rule into the ETL — if the allocation rule changes, historical rows must be reprocessed. This is generally preferable to a bridge only when the fact table is used primarily for promotion-level aggregation rather than transaction-level accuracy.

Option D (promotion_coverage_fact) is a reasonable design for question (a) and (b) but doesn't directly answer question (c) — revenue lift — without joining back to the sales fact. It creates two separate fact tables that analysts must join, adding query complexity. It's also effectively a bridge table with a different name; making it a separate 'fact' table is semantically misleading when it represents a dimensional relationship, not a business event.
hints: Many-to-many relationships between a dimension and an external entity are a canonical problem in dimensional modeling — there is a well-established pattern that avoids duplicating fact rows.
A weight factor in the bridge table is needed to allocate measures (like revenue) fairly when a single transaction is covered by multiple entities on the other side of the many-to-many.
Consider the implications of duplicating fact rows to handle multi-promotion transactions — what happens to SUM(revenue) in a query that doesn't filter on promotion_id?

title: dbt Incremental Strategy for Late-Arriving Event Data
scenario_context: A streaming analytics team at a SaaS company uses dbt to model a user_events table ingested from Kafka via a batch landing zone. Events can arrive up to 72 hours late due to mobile clients with intermittent connectivity. The dbt incremental model currently uses `unique_key = 'event_id'` and `incremental_strategy = 'merge'` on the partition key `event_date`. The model runs hourly. Data engineers are noticing that late-arriving events that fall outside the current merge window (events with event_date older than today - 1) are being missed — they land in the raw layer but never make it into the incremental model because the merge only scans recent partitions.
description: What is the correct dbt incremental strategy to handle events that can arrive up to 72 hours late while keeping hourly run time acceptable?
options: Option A — Extend the incremental scan window to cover the last 4 days using a `_dbt_max_partition_date` filter in the `is_incremental()` block: `WHERE event_date >= current_date - 4`. Use `unique_key = 'event_id'` with merge strategy. This ensures late arrivals within 72 hours are always within the scan window, with acceptable hourly reprocessing cost on a 4-day window.

Option B — Switch to `incremental_strategy = 'insert_overwrite'` with `partitions_to_replace` covering the last 4 days. This avoids the merge overhead but requires careful partition alignment to avoid overwriting valid data outside the replacement window.

Option C — Run the incremental model on a 1-day window for hourly runs, and schedule a separate nightly full-refresh run to catch all late arrivals. The full refresh ensures correctness; the hourly incremental provides near-real-time freshness for recent events.

Option D — Add a `loaded_at` column (pipeline ingestion timestamp) and use it as the incremental key instead of `event_date`. Scan for `loaded_at >= last_run_timestamp` to capture all newly landed records regardless of their event_date. This correctly handles late arrivals without widening the event_date window.
explanation:
Option D is correct. The root cause of late-arrival misses is using event_date as the incremental boundary. Late-arriving events have an old event_date but a recent loaded_at (pipeline ingestion timestamp). By switching the incremental scan key to loaded_at >= last_run_timestamp, every newly landed record — regardless of how old its event_date is — will be captured in the next hourly run. This is the standard pattern for event pipelines with late-arriving data. The merge on unique_key = 'event_id' correctly handles deduplication if an event lands multiple times.

Option A (widening the event_date window to 4 days) is the most common expert-level fix attempt. It works, but it's inefficient: every hourly run rescans 4 days of partitions, even when there are no late arrivals in that window. As data volume grows, the hourly reprocessing cost grows linearly with the window. More critically, if an event arrives 73 hours late (just outside the 4-day window), it is still missed — the fundamental problem is not solved, just deferred.

Option B (insert_overwrite on a 4-day window) has the same coverage problem as A but with even higher rewrite overhead: it replaces entire 4-day partitions on every hourly run, which is expensive and increases the risk of data loss if the replacement job fails mid-run.

Option C (nightly full refresh as a catch-up) is operationally pragmatic but introduces a correctness gap: late arrivals between the nightly runs can affect metrics that downstream consumers read hourly. For a SaaS product with revenue-impacting event analytics, a 24-hour correctness gap is typically unacceptable. It also adds operational complexity (two separate jobs for one model) and doesn't eliminate the need for the full-refresh run to be monitored independently.
hints: The incremental boundary determines which source records are scanned on each run — consider whether the current boundary (event_date) correctly identifies all newly landed records regardless of when the event occurred.
Late-arriving events have a recent pipeline ingestion timestamp but an old event timestamp — which column should drive the incremental scan to capture them without widening a time window?
Using a loaded_at or ingested_at timestamp as the incremental key is a standard pattern for event pipelines with late data — it decouples the incremental boundary from event time entirely.

title: Choosing Between Lake, Warehouse, and Lakehouse for ML + BI Workloads
scenario_context: A mid-size healthcare analytics company has two primary data consumers: (1) a BI team that uses Tableau to build operational dashboards over structured claims data (SQL queries, sub-second response expected, governed schema), and (2) a data science team that trains ML models on raw clinical notes (unstructured text), claims records, and lab results (semi-structured JSON). The current architecture is a data lake on S3 with raw parquet files. The BI team complains of slow queries and schema inconsistency. The DS team wants richer feature engineering on raw data without a copy step. Regulatory requirements mandate row-level access control and a full audit trail of data access.
description: Which storage architecture best serves both teams' workloads while meeting the regulatory requirements?
options: Option A — Adopt a lakehouse architecture (e.g., Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg on S3) with a SQL engine (e.g., Trino or Databricks SQL) on top. The lakehouse provides ACID transactions, schema enforcement for BI queries, and direct raw-file access for ML — eliminating the copy step. Row-level security and audit logging are implemented at the table/engine layer.

Option B — Maintain the data lake for DS workloads and add a cloud data warehouse (e.g., Snowflake or BigQuery) for BI. Sync structured data from the lake to the warehouse on a nightly basis. Each team uses the system optimized for its workload; governance is enforced independently in each system.

Option C — Move all data to a cloud data warehouse. Warehouse the structured claims and JSON lab results using variant/JSON column types; store clinical notes as text columns. Enforce row-level security via warehouse RLS policies. DS teams query the warehouse directly using SQL-based feature engineering.

Option D — Build a streaming lakehouse with Apache Kafka as the ingestion backbone and Apache Flink for real-time transformations. Structured claims arrive in the warehouse via CDC; raw data lands in S3. Real-time governance is enforced via Flink's stream processing policies.
explanation:
Option A is correct. A lakehouse architecture (Delta Lake or Iceberg on S3 with a SQL engine) directly addresses all stated requirements. For the BI team: ACID transactions and schema enforcement provide the schema consistency they lack in a raw parquet lake, and SQL engines like Databricks SQL or Trino provide sub-second query performance on structured data via caching and vectorized execution. For the DS team: they access the same storage layer without a copy step, reading raw parquet or delta files directly for ML feature engineering. Row-level security (via column masking and access policies at the engine layer) and audit logging (via Delta log / Iceberg metadata) satisfy regulatory requirements without duplicating data across systems.

Option B (dual-system: lake + warehouse) is the most tempting expert-level alternative. It works and is widely used. However, it introduces a nightly sync that creates a 24-hour freshness lag for BI, requires governing two separate access control systems (doubling audit complexity), and inevitably leads to schema drift between the lake and warehouse versions of the same data. For a healthcare setting with strict audit requirements, managing two independent governance stacks is a significant operational risk.

Option C (everything in the warehouse) forces clinical notes (unstructured text, potentially gigabytes per document) and raw JSON into a column store optimized for structured analytics. Warehouses are expensive for storing and querying large unstructured text, and many ML frameworks cannot efficiently read training data from warehouse tables — they need file-based access. This creates friction for the DS team and may violate data residency requirements by moving raw clinical data into a SaaS warehouse.

Option D (streaming lakehouse with Kafka/Flink) introduces significant operational complexity that is not justified by the stated requirements. There is no mention of real-time BI or streaming ML. Adding Kafka and Flink for a batch BI + batch ML workload creates an over-engineered architecture with higher cost and operational burden than the problem requires.
hints: Consider which architecture eliminates the data copy step between the layer serving ML and the layer serving BI — a copy step means two governance systems and two sources of truth.
Regulatory requirements for row-level access control and audit trails are easier to enforce when there is a single storage layer with a unified policy engine rather than two separate systems.

A lakehouse (Delta Lake / Iceberg) provides ACID, schema enforcement, and time-travel on top of object storage — evaluate whether this closes the BI team's complaints without requiring a separate warehouse.

title: Schema Design from Ambiguous Subscription + Usage Requirements
scenario_context: A SaaS company tracks subscription plans and per-seat usage. The product team provides these requirements: (1) each account can have multiple subscriptions over time (plan upgrades, downgrades, cancellations), (2) each subscription has a fixed monthly fee and a per-seat usage charge above a base seat count, (3) analysts need to compute monthly recurring revenue (MRR) and seat utilization for each account, and (4) historical subscription terms must be preserved for audit purposes. A data architect proposes two candidate models: (A) a subscription_fact table at the grain of (account_id, subscription_id, billing_month) with pre-computed MRR and seat_count columns, or (B) a subscription_dim (SCD Type 2) containing plan terms, joined to a monthly_usage_fact at the grain of (account_id, billing_month) containing actual seat counts.
description: Which schema design correctly models subscription-based SaaS metrics while satisfying the MRR, utilization, and audit requirements?
options: Option A — The subscription_dim (SCD Type 2) + monthly_usage_fact design is correct. Subscription terms (plan, price, base seats) are a slowly changing dimension with full history. Monthly seat usage is a measurable fact. MRR is computed by joining usage to the subscription dim valid on that billing month. Audit requirement is satisfied by Type 2 history.

Option B — The subscription_fact design is correct. Billing month is the natural grain; pre-computing MRR and seat_count avoids join complexity. Subscription term changes are captured by new rows with different subscription_id values. Audit is satisfied by the append-only nature of the fact table.

Option C — Combine both: use a subscription_header_dim (Type 1, current state) for fast lookups, a subscription_history table (append-only log of term changes) for audit, and the monthly_usage_fact for seat counts. MRR is pre-computed in a dbt model joining all three.

Option D — Model subscriptions as a single subscription_event_fact at the grain of (account_id, event_type, event_date) where event_type includes 'plan_start', 'plan_change', 'seat_add', and 'cancellation'. Derive MRR and utilization by replaying events in order. This preserves maximum audit detail.
explanation:
Option A is correct. The subscription_dim (SCD Type 2) + monthly_usage_fact design correctly separates concerns: subscription terms (plan name, monthly fee, base seat count, effective dates) are a slowly changing attribute of the subscription entity, and SCD Type 2 preserves the full history of term changes for audit. Monthly seat usage is a measured fact (how many seats were actually used in a given billing month). MRR for a given billing month is computed by joining the monthly_usage_fact to the subscription_dim row that was valid on that month's start date — a standard point-in-time join. This approach keeps the fact table lean (one row per account per month) and the dimension table historically accurate.

Option B (subscription_fact with pre-computed MRR) is tempting because it avoids the point-in-time join. However, pre-computing MRR embeds business logic (fixed_fee + max(0, seats - base_seats) × per_seat_price) into the ETL. If the pricing formula changes retroactively, all historical rows must be reprocessed. More importantly, new rows with different subscription_ids when terms change means analysts must be careful about double-counting or gaps when a subscription transitions mid-month. The fact table grain is ambiguous for the transition period.

Option C (three-table design) adds complexity without commensurate benefit. A Type 1 header dim plus a separate history log is essentially an ad-hoc reimplementation of SCD Type 2. Maintaining two representations of subscription state (current + log) doubles the risk of drift between them. The dbt model joining three tables for MRR is more fragile than a clean Type 2 + fact design.

Option D (event-sourced fact) is the most technically sophisticated option but the least analytically practical. Deriving MRR and seat utilization by replaying events in order at query time is expensive (window functions over unbounded event history) and requires all analysts to understand the event replay semantics. Event sourcing is a valid ingestion pattern but should be materialized into an aggregated model (like Option A) for analytical consumption, not queried directly.
hints: Identify which data elements describe a business entity's configuration that changes infrequently (subscription terms) versus measurements that accumulate regularly (monthly seat usage) — these belong in different table types.
A point-in-time join between a monthly usage fact and a SCD Type 2 dimension gives you the correct subscription terms for any billing month without pre-computing business logic into the ETL.
Pre-computing MRR in the fact table bakes a pricing formula into historical rows — consider what happens when that formula needs to change retroactively.

title: Data Vault Link Design for Multi-Party Financial Transactions
scenario_context: A payments platform processes transactions that involve exactly three parties: a payer (individual or business), a payee (individual or business), and an intermediary bank. Each party is identified by its own source-system key. The analytics team needs to model transaction history in a Data Vault. A data architect proposes a Transaction Link with three foreign keys: payer_hashkey, payee_hashkey, and bank_hashkey. A second architect argues that payers and payees should share a single Party Hub (since both can be individuals or businesses), while the bank should be a separate Institution Hub. A third argues for three separate Hubs (Payer, Payee, Bank) even if payers and payees share the same entity type.
description: Which Data Vault link and hub design correctly models multi-party financial transactions where payer and payee are the same entity type but different business roles?
options: Option A — One Party Hub (covers both payers and payees, since they are the same type of entity) and one Institution Hub (for banks). The Transaction Link has three foreign keys: payer_party_hashkey, payee_party_hashkey, and bank_hashkey. Separate hashkeys for the same Hub allow the link to capture role-specific context without separate Hubs.

Option B — Three separate Hubs: Payer Hub, Payee Hub, and Bank Hub. Even though payers and payees are the same entity type, their business keys may differ by source system, so maintaining separate Hubs preserves source fidelity. The Transaction Link references all three.

Option C — One Party Hub and one Institution Hub, but the Transaction Link is split into two links: a Payer-Transaction Link and a Payee-Transaction Link. This avoids the ambiguity of having two foreign keys pointing to the same Hub in one link.

Option D — A single Transaction Hub (keyed on transaction_id) with Party Satellites and Bank Satellites attached, storing payer/payee/bank identifiers as Satellite attributes rather than Hub foreign keys. This avoids complex link design.
explanation:
Option A is correct. In Data Vault, Hubs represent business concepts (entities), not roles. Payers and payees are both 'parties' (individuals or businesses) — they share the same business concept. Separating them into different Hubs because they play different roles in a transaction would violate the principle that a Hub represents a unique business key for one type of real-world entity. The solution is a single Party Hub with role-specific foreign key aliases in the Transaction Link (payer_party_hashkey and payee_party_hashkey both reference the Party Hub). This is a standard Data Vault pattern called a 'same-hub role link' and is explicitly supported in Data Vault 2.0 methodology.

Option B (three separate Hubs) is the most common mistake. Separating Payer and Payee into different Hubs because 'business keys may differ by source system' conflates the source key (which belongs in the Hub's business key column) with the business concept. If a company appears as both a payer in one transaction and a payee in another, they would have two different Hub rows in two different Hubs — breaking the golden rule that a Hub represents a unique business entity. Cross-role analysis (e.g., 'which companies are both frequent payers and payees?') would require joining two different Hubs.

Option C (split into two links) is an over-normalization that actually loses information. A transaction's payer and payee are meaningfully related within the same transaction event. Splitting into two links requires a Transaction Hub as the joining entity, adds complexity, and makes it harder to query 'who paid whom in transaction X' — the most fundamental question about a payment transaction.

Option D (Party Satellites on a Transaction Hub) inverts the Data Vault design. Transaction is an event (a Link), not a Hub. Payer and payee are entities (Hubs), not Satellite attributes. Storing entity identifiers in Satellites rather than as Hub references breaks the hashkey-based join pattern and prevents clean lineage tracking of party history.
hints: Consider whether payers and payees represent fundamentally different types of business entities, or simply different roles the same entity type can play — this distinction determines how many entity tables you need.
A Link table can contain multiple foreign key references to the same Hub using role-specific aliases — this is a documented Data Vault pattern for self-referencing or role-playing relationships.
If a company can appear as both payer and payee across different transactions, which Hub design allows you to query that company's full history regardless of role?

title: Partitioning Strategy for a 10-Billion-Row Event Fact Table
scenario_context: A media streaming company has a user_events fact table in BigQuery with 10 billion rows covering 3 years of history. The table records every play, pause, skip, and search event. Query patterns are: (1) product analysts query the last 7 days of events filtered by event_type, (2) data scientists run full-history queries for a specific user_id (cohort analysis), (3) billing computes monthly aggregates by subscription_tier. The table currently has no partitioning or clustering. P95 query time is 4 minutes; cost per product analyst query is $18.
description: Which partitioning and clustering strategy best reduces query cost and latency for all three workload types?
options: Option A — Partition by event_date (daily) and cluster by (event_type, user_id). Product analysts benefit from partition pruning on the last 7 days; clustering on event_type provides additional micro-partition pruning within those partitions. Data scientist cohort queries benefit from clustering on user_id. Billing monthly aggregates use partition pruning on event_date ranges.

Option B — Partition by subscription_tier (a low-cardinality column) and cluster by event_date. Billing queries benefit from tier partition pruning. Product analyst queries must scan all tiers (since they don't filter by tier) but benefit from clustering on event_date for recency filtering.

Option C — Partition by event_date and cluster by (user_id, event_type). User_id is placed first in clustering to optimize the data scientist cohort queries, which are the most expensive queries by scan volume. Product analyst queries and billing queries also benefit from partition pruning.

Option D — Use range partitioning on user_id (bucketed into 100 ranges) and cluster by event_date. This optimizes data scientist cohort queries by partitioning on the most selective filter dimension. Product analyst queries must scan all user_id partitions.
explanation:
Option A is correct. Partitioning by event_date (daily) is the right choice because two of the three workloads (product analysts querying last 7 days, billing computing monthly aggregates) are date-bounded. Date partitioning is the most universally impactful strategy for time-series event data. Clustering by (event_type, user_id) in that order serves both remaining workloads: product analysts filter heavily by event_type (the first cluster column, providing the strongest within-partition pruning), and data scientists filter by user_id (second cluster column, still beneficial within each date partition). Billing monthly aggregates use partition pruning across date ranges and do not need the cluster columns.

Option C is the primary distractor: it uses the same partition but reverses the cluster column order to (user_id, event_type). In BigQuery, clustering column order matters — the first column provides the most pruning. Data scientist cohort queries are described as expensive by scan volume, but the question asks for the strategy that benefits ALL THREE workloads. Product analysts filtering by event_type get much better pruning when event_type is the first cluster column (they scan only the event_type micro-partition within each date partition). Reversing to user_id first makes product analyst queries scan across all user_id clusters within each date partition before filtering on event_type.

Option B partitions on subscription_tier, a low-cardinality column (likely 3–5 values). Partitioning on a low-cardinality column creates very large partitions that don't prune effectively. Product analyst queries that don't filter by tier must scan all partitions, which is worse than no partitioning at all for their workload.

Option D (range partitioning on user_id) optimizes only the data scientist cohort queries and is harmful for the other two workloads. Product analyst queries must scan all 100 user_id partitions; billing queries must do the same. User_id-based partitioning is rarely appropriate for event tables because the vast majority of queries are time-bounded, not user-bounded.
hints: Consider which filter dimension is shared by the largest number of workload types — that column is typically the best partition key for an event table.

Clustering column order in BigQuery determines which column provides the strongest micro-partition pruning — put the column with the highest query filter selectivity first among the workloads you most want to optimize.
Low-cardinality columns (like subscription_tier with 3–5 values) make poor partition keys because each partition remains very large, limiting the benefit of partition pruning.

title: Handling Hierarchy Ragged-Depth in an Organizational Dimension
scenario_context: A global manufacturing company has an organizational hierarchy with ragged depth: some business units have 3 levels (Region → Country → Plant), others have 4 levels (Region → Country → Division → Plant), and headquarters has only 1 level (Global). Analysts need to: (a) roll up sales to any hierarchy level, (b) filter a report by any node in the hierarchy, and (c) perform parent-child comparison (compare a country's sales against its region's total). The current model is a fixed-depth dimension with NULL-padded columns (level_1 through level_5). Analysts complain that NULL-padding forces them to write COALESCE chains in every rollup query.
description: Which hierarchy modeling approach best handles variable-depth organizational hierarchies for analytical rollup, filtering, and parent-child comparison?
options: Option A — Model the hierarchy as a closure table (also called a bridge table of ancestors): one row per (ancestor_node_id, descendant_node_id, depth) pair. Every node is its own ancestor at depth 0. Rollup queries join on ancestor_node_id; filtering on any level is a depth=0 self-join; parent-child comparison joins on depth=1.

Option B — Use a fixed-depth dimension with NULL-padded level columns (level_1 through level_5) and add a 'leaf_level' integer column indicating the actual depth of each node. Analysts use the leaf_level column to avoid COALESCE chains by selecting the appropriate level column dynamically.

Option C — Normalize the hierarchy into a parent_node dimension table (node_id, parent_node_id, node_name, node_level). Use recursive CTEs at query time to perform rollups and ancestor lookups. This is the most normalized representation and avoids data duplication.

Option D — Denormalize the hierarchy by pre-computing a materialized path (e.g., '/Global/Region_A/Country_US/Plant_7') as a VARCHAR column on the leaf node. Pattern matching (LIKE '/Global/Region_A/%') performs rollups; string parsing extracts individual levels.
explanation:
Option A is correct. The closure table (ancestor bridge) pattern is the optimal solution for ragged hierarchies in an analytical warehouse. Pre-computing all (ancestor, descendant, depth) pairs allows rollup queries to be simple equi-joins on ancestor_node_id without recursion or COALESCE chains. Filtering by any node — regardless of its depth in the hierarchy — is the same query structure. Parent-child comparisons join on depth=1 pairs. Because all ancestor relationships are materialized, query performance is predictable and doesn't degrade with hierarchy depth. The tradeoff is that the closure table has O(n²) rows in the worst case, but for organizational hierarchies of tens of thousands of nodes this is entirely manageable.

Option B (fixed-depth with leaf_level) is the current approach with a minor improvement. Adding leaf_level reduces COALESCE usage but doesn't eliminate it — queries for rollup still need conditional logic to select the right level column. It also doesn't handle ragged depth gracefully: a 3-level node has NULLs in levels 4 and 5 that must be handled carefully. This is a band-aid on a fundamentally flawed design.

Option C (recursive CTE at query time) is the most normalized design and is correct for OLTP or small-scale analytics. However, recursive CTEs at query time over large fact tables are expensive and non-deterministic in performance. Most analytical warehouses have limited optimization for recursive queries. Pre-computing the closure table moves the recursion to load time (cheap, done once) rather than query time (expensive, done on every query). For an analytical workload with potentially thousands of concurrent queries, recursive CTEs are not scalable.

Option D (materialized path as VARCHAR) allows rollup via LIKE pattern matching, which works for simple use cases. However, LIKE '%pattern%' queries cannot use column statistics or indexes, requiring full column scans. Pattern matching for parent-child comparison (extracting the path segment one level above) requires string manipulation that varies by level and is error-prone. This approach also conflates hierarchy position (a structural concept) with a string representation (a display concept), making it brittle when nodes are renamed or reorganized.
hints: Consider which approach materializes all ancestor-descendant relationships at load time versus computing them at query time — and which of those is more appropriate for high-concurrency analytical queries.

A closure table (ancestor bridge) pre-computes every ancestor-descendant pair with depth metadata, enabling rollup and filter queries to use simple equi-joins without recursion or string manipulation.

Recursive CTEs are elegant for small hierarchies but can be expensive at query time in analytical warehouses — evaluate whether pre-materialization of the hierarchy structure is feasible given the hierarchy size.

title: Referential Integrity Under High-Volume Parallel Loads
scenario_context: A ride-sharing company loads 50 million trip records per day into a dimensional model in Redshift. The trips fact table references a driver dimension and a rider dimension. The ETL pipeline uses parallel COPY commands (8 concurrent streams). During parallel loads, fact rows occasionally arrive before the corresponding dimension rows are committed, causing orphaned fact rows (fact rows with no matching dimension key). The team tried enabling Redshift's foreign key constraints but found they blocked parallel loads and reduced throughput by 60%. They are evaluating alternatives to maintain referential integrity without sacrificing load performance.
description: Which approach correctly manages referential integrity for a high-volume parallel-load dimensional model in Redshift?
options: Option A — Disable Redshift foreign key constraints (they are unenforced anyway). Enforce referential integrity via a post-load dbt test that checks for orphaned fact rows after every ETL run. If orphans are found, backfill missing dimension rows from source before the next reporting window opens.

Option B — Implement a staging-based load pattern: load all dimension rows first into staging tables, run a MERGE/UPSERT to the dimension tables, then load fact rows. A pipeline dependency (step ordering) ensures dimensions are always committed before facts. Foreign key constraints remain declared but unenforced.

Option C — Add a fact row quarantine table: fact rows that fail a pre-load referential check are routed to a quarantine table. The main pipeline retries quarantined rows every hour. Orphaned rows that are not resolved within 24 hours are dropped and logged.

Option D — Use a surrogate key lookup table to buffer all incoming fact rows. On each hourly batch, resolve surrogate keys only for fact rows where the corresponding dimension row exists. Hold unresolved rows in the buffer until the dimension row arrives (up to 48 hours). Load resolved rows into the final fact table.
explanation:
Option B is correct. The root cause of orphaned fact rows is a race condition: fact rows arriving before dimension rows during parallel loads. The correct fix is a pipeline dependency that guarantees dimension rows are committed before any fact rows that reference them are loaded. This is implemented as a staging-based pattern: (1) load all dimension data into staging, (2) UPSERT dimensions to the production dimension tables, (3) only then load fact rows. This eliminates the race condition structurally. Foreign key constraints can remain declared as informational metadata (useful for query optimizer and documentation) without being enforced — Redshift's unenforced constraints don't block throughput when they're informational. Post-load dbt tests serve as a safety net for any edge cases the ordering misses.

Option A (post-load dbt tests + backfill) is a reactive approach that allows orphaned rows to exist in the fact table until the test runs and the backfill completes. During this window, queries on the fact table can return incorrect join results. For a ride-sharing company, this means incorrect trip metrics visible to analysts. The orphan window is unacceptable for operational reporting.

Option C (quarantine table with 24-hour retry) introduces operational complexity: a quarantine queue that must be monitored, retried, and eventually drained. It also accepts that some fact rows may be permanently dropped (after 24 hours) — losing business data. For a financial transaction type workload (trips = revenue events), dropping orphaned rows is not acceptable.

Option D (surrogate key buffer) is technically sophisticated but adds significant latency and complexity. Fact rows can be held in the buffer for up to 48 hours — a reporting model that holds trip records for 48 hours before loading them is unacceptable for operational dashboards. The buffer also requires its own storage, retry logic, and monitoring infrastructure. The fundamental problem (a race condition between dimension and fact loads) is better solved by sequencing the loads correctly (Option B) rather than by buffering.
hints: Orphaned fact rows in a parallel load scenario are a race condition problem — consider which solution addresses the root cause (load ordering) rather than the symptom (orphaned rows in the table).
Redshift foreign key constraints are informational and do not block loads when declared — they can be retained for optimizer hints without impacting throughput.

A staging-based load pattern with explicit step dependencies ensures dimensions are always committed before the facts that reference them — this is the standard pattern for dimensional model ETL pipelines.

title: SCD Type 4 vs. Type 6 for a High-Churn Customer Attribute
scenario_context: A telecommunications company's customer dimension includes a 'plan_tier' attribute (Basic, Standard, Premium) that changes frequently — an average customer changes tier 4 times per year. The dimension has 8 million customers. Analysts need: (1) historical accuracy for closed billing periods (what tier was this customer on in March?), (2) fast current-tier queries for real-time dashboards, and (3) minimal storage growth from the high-churn attribute. The team currently uses SCD Type 2 for all attributes, resulting in a customer dimension with an average of 12 rows per customer (96 million rows total). Query performance on current-tier lookups is degrading because BI tools scan all rows before filtering on is_current.
description: Which SCD hybrid strategy best addresses historical accuracy, current-tier query performance, and storage growth caused by a high-churn attribute?
options: Option A — Implement SCD Type 4 (mini-dimension) for plan_tier: extract it into a separate plan_history mini-dimension table at the grain of (customer_id, tier_change_date). The main customer dimension is Type 1 (current state only, one row per customer). Current-tier queries hit the main dimension; historical queries join to the mini-dimension.

Option B — Implement SCD Type 6 (hybrid): keep the main customer dimension as Type 2 with valid_from/valid_to, add a current_tier column (updated in-place on all rows on every tier change). Current-tier queries use the current_tier column without filtering on is_current; historical queries use valid_from/valid_to.

Option C — Split the customer dimension into two: a stable_customer_dim (Type 2 for slowly changing attributes like name, address, DOB — rarely changes) and a volatile_customer_dim (Type 1 for plan_tier, updated in place). Current-tier queries hit the volatile dim; historical billing queries join the stable dim to a separate tier_change_log.

Option D — Keep the existing SCD Type 2 design but add a materialized view filtered to is_current = true. The materialized view refreshes incrementally on each tier change event. BI tools query the materialized view for current-tier lookups; the full dimension table remains the source for historical queries.
explanation:
Option A is correct. SCD Type 4 is designed exactly for this scenario: a high-churn attribute that bloats the main dimension with frequent row additions. By extracting plan_tier into a mini-dimension (plan_history table) at the (customer_id, tier_change_date) grain, the main customer dimension shrinks back to 8 million rows (one per customer, current state only). Current-tier lookups are fast single-row lookups on the main dimension. Historical billing queries join to the plan_history mini-dimension for the tier effective on a specific date. Storage growth is isolated to the plan_history table, which grows proportionally to tier changes rather than inflating the entire customer dimension.

Option B (Type 6) addresses the current-tier performance problem by adding a current_tier column, but it does NOT reduce storage growth. The dimension still has 96 million rows (12 per customer on average). Type 6 adds a current_tier column that is updated on every row on each tier change — for 8M customers × 12 average rows, that's 96M row updates on every tier change, which is extremely expensive at the update rate described (4 changes/year × 8M customers = 32M updates/year to every historical row). Type 6 is appropriate when the main dimension doesn't have excessive row growth; here the row count is the primary problem.

Option C (splitting into stable and volatile dimensions) is a reasonable approach but introduces a tier_change_log as a third object that analysts must know to query for historical accuracy. The 'volatile_customer_dim' as Type 1 solves the current-tier query problem but requires joining to the tier_change_log for historical queries — which is effectively what Option A's mini-dimension already does, with less architectural complexity.

Option D (materialized view on is_current) is a good tactical fix for query performance but doesn't address storage growth. The underlying dimension still has 96M rows. The materialized view must be refreshed incrementally — for a dim that has tier changes 32M times/year, incremental refresh of the MV has significant overhead and may not achieve sub-second latency for real-time dashboards.
hints: When a single high-churn attribute is causing the majority of row growth in a large dimension, consider whether that attribute should be separated from the stable attributes rather than co-located in the same versioned history table.

SCD Type 4 extracts the frequently changing attribute into a separate history table while keeping the main dimension lean (one row per entity, current state only) — evaluate this against the stated requirement to minimize storage growth.

SCD Type 6 addresses current-value query performance but does not reduce row count — it adds a column to all existing rows. Evaluate whether reducing row count or adding columns better addresses the stated problems.

title: Modeling Customer Lifetime Value in a Dimensional Schema
scenario_context: A subscription e-commerce company wants to add Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) to their dimensional model. CLV is defined as the sum of all past revenue plus a 12-month forward revenue prediction from a Python ML model. The ML model is retrained weekly and the predicted CLV can change significantly between retrainings. Analysts need: (1) current CLV for segmentation (fast lookup), (2) CLV trend over time (how has CLV changed per customer over the past year?), (3) a breakout of historical actual revenue vs. predicted revenue for audit. The data engineering team debates where CLV belongs: in the customer dimension, in a CLV fact table, or as a derived measure in a dbt model.
description: Where should Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) live in the dimensional model, given the requirements for segmentation, trend analysis, and audit breakout?
options: Option A — A separate clv_snapshots fact table at the grain of (customer_id, snapshot_date), containing actual_revenue_to_date and predicted_12m_revenue columns. Current CLV is the latest snapshot row; trend analysis uses window functions on snapshot_date; audit breakout uses the two separate columns.

Option B — A CLV column added to the customer dimension as SCD Type 1 (overwrite on each weekly model retraining). Historical CLV trend is captured in a separate customer_clv_history table populated by a dbt snapshot. Current CLV is a fast single-row lookup from the dimension.

Option C — CLV as a derived measure in a dbt mart model that computes it on-the-fly by summing actual revenue from the orders fact and adding the latest prediction from a separate model_predictions table. No CLV is stored; it is computed at query time for any date range.

Option D — A CLV column on the customer dimension as SCD Type 2: each weekly retraining adds a new dimension row with the new CLV value. The valid_from/valid_to range captures the period each CLV estimate was 'current'. Trend analysis uses date-range filtering on the dimension.
explanation:
Option A is correct. CLV combines two distinct measures (historical actual revenue and forward prediction) that change at different frequencies and for different reasons. A clv_snapshots fact table at the (customer_id, snapshot_date) grain is the right design because: (1) it is a measured, time-stamped value — a fact, not a dimensional attribute; (2) snapshot_date enables trend analysis via simple time-series queries without date-range joins; (3) separate actual_revenue_to_date and predicted_12m_revenue columns provide the audit breakout; and (4) the latest snapshot row gives current CLV for segmentation queries. The weekly retraining produces a new snapshot row rather than overwriting history.

Option B (SCD Type 1 on customer dim + history table) is a common but incorrect pattern. CLV is not a descriptive attribute of a customer — it is a computed metric that changes over time. Storing it in the customer dimension conflates entity attributes (who is the customer?) with measurements (what is their value?). The separate history table is a workaround that is effectively a reimplementation of the fact table from Option A with more complexity.

Option D (SCD Type 2 on customer dim) has the same conceptual problem as B: CLV is a measurement, not a slowly changing attribute. Using SCD Type 2 for CLV inflates the customer dimension with a new row every week per customer — for 10M customers retrained weekly, that's 10M new dimension rows per week (520M rows/year). Trend analysis requires date-range filtering on the dimension, which is less efficient and semantically awkward than time-series queries on a fact table.

Option C (derived at query time) is appealing for its simplicity but is computationally expensive — summing all historical revenue per customer from the orders fact table on every CLV query is an O(n) operation per customer, prohibitive for segmentation queries that need CLV for all 10M customers simultaneously. It also requires joining to a separate model_predictions table with its own versioning challenges. Pre-materializing CLV in a fact table (Option A) is specifically designed to avoid this query-time computation.
hints: Consider whether CLV is a descriptive attribute of the customer entity (belongs in a dimension) or a measured value that changes over time (belongs in a fact) — the distinction determines the right location.
A fact table at the grain of (customer, snapshot_date) naturally supports trend analysis, current-value lookup, and the two-column audit breakout without needing a secondary history table.

Storing a computed metric in the customer dimension as SCD Type 2 conflates entity identity with measurement versioning — how would a 10M-customer dimension behave with weekly CLV updates over 2 years?

title: dbt Materialization Strategy for a Funnel Model with Backfill Requirements
scenario_context: A growth team at a B2B SaaS company uses a dbt funnel model to compute account-level stage progression (Lead → Trial → Opportunity → Closed Won/Lost). The funnel model joins five upstream tables: accounts, contacts, activities, opportunities, and deals. The model currently runs as a view. Each query takes 90 seconds due to the join complexity and 200M source rows. The team wants to: (1) run the funnel model in production with sub-10-second query time, (2) support ad-hoc historical backfills when CRM data is corrected retroactively, (3) avoid full rebuilds of 3 years of history on each daily run. A data engineer proposes converting the model to incremental with `unique_key = 'account_id'` and `incremental_strategy = 'merge'`.
description: What is the correct dbt materialization strategy for a complex funnel model that requires fast queries, retroactive backfill support, and efficient daily updates?
options: Option A — Materialize as a table with full refresh on a daily schedule. Combine with a separate incremental 'delta' model that processes only yesterday's changed accounts (using a CRM updated_at timestamp). For backfills, run the full-refresh model with a date range parameter. Sub-10-second queries come from the pre-materialized table.

Option B — Materialize as incremental with `unique_key = 'account_id'` and `incremental_strategy = 'merge'`. Add a `--full-refresh` flag to the backfill pipeline. The merge strategy handles retroactive corrections by overwriting the existing account row on each run. Daily incremental runs process only accounts updated since the last run.
