The ERP system performs a vendor consolidation: vendor V003 is merged into V001. All records in the ERP — including historical ones — are retroactively updated to reference V001. The following week, Finance reports that vendor V001's historical revenue has roughly doubled, and V003 shows zero revenue for all past periods.
description: What caused the misattribution, and which modeling practice would have prevented it?
options: Vendor consolidation is a source system data quality issue — the same misattribution would occur regardless of which key strategy the warehouse used, because the source system changed the underlying data.

Using the ERP's natural vendor_id as the fact table foreign key means the warehouse inherits retroactive ERP updates — historical fact rows that originally referenced V003 now resolve to V001 in every join. A warehouse-generated key for each vendor (independent of ERP identifiers) would have kept V003 rows pointing to the original V003 dimension row, preserving historical attribution.
The root cause is that dim_vendor was not rebuilt after the consolidation — re-running the dimension ETL with a deduplication step would restore the correct historical vendor rows.
The fix is to store both old and new vendor_ids in dim_vendor using a cross-reference column — fact rows join to the cross-reference table at query time to resolve historical attribution.
explanation: When the ERP retroactively changed all V003 references to V001, the fact rows in fact_purchase that stored 'V003' as the foreign key now mismatch dim_vendor (which was updated to only show V001). Depending on the JOIN type, those rows either resolve incorrectly to V001 or drop entirely. If a warehouse-generated dimension key had been used — one that was created when V003 first appeared and never changed — the old fact rows would still hold that key and join correctly to the V003 dimension row, regardless of what the ERP did to its own identifier. Option 1 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: the misattribution is specifically a modeling choice — using a natural key that the source system can retroactively change without notifying the warehouse. A warehouse-generated key is immutable by warehouse policy and would have isolated the fact from the ERP change. Option 2 is wrong: re-running the dimension ETL after consolidation would produce a dim_vendor with only V001 (the consolidated entity), which makes historical attribution even harder — the original V003 entry is gone from the source and cannot be recovered. Option 3 is wrong: a cross-reference table at query time introduces join complexity and still relies on the source system having preserved the old V003 identifier — if the ERP retroactively overwrote it everywhere, the cross-reference has nothing to link back to.
hints: When fact rows use the ERP's vendor identifier directly as a foreign key, what happens to those fact rows when the ERP retroactively renames or merges that identifier?

A warehouse key generated at the time a vendor first appears is never changed by the warehouse team — even if the source system merges two vendors. What would historical V003 fact rows show if they referenced that warehouse-generated key instead of the ERP vendor_id?

title: Debug an inflated quarterly balance by identifying incorrect aggregation of a semi-additive measure across time
scenario_context: A finance team builds fact_account_balance as a monthly periodic snapshot: one row per account per month-end, storing the account's end-of-month balance. An analyst queries total deposits held across all accounts for Q1 2024 by writing: SELECT SUM(balance) FROM fact_account_balance WHERE snapshot_month IN ('2024-01', '2024-02', '2024-03'). The result is approximately 3× the figure shown in the bank's general ledger for March 31.
description: What is the structural cause of the inflation, and what is the correct query approach for quarterly total deposits?
options: The IN clause includes 3 months; each account has 3 snapshot rows in the range; SUM(balance) adds each account's balance three times — once for January, once for February, once for March. The correct approach for a point-in-time balance is to filter to a single month-end snapshot, not sum across multiple months.

The periodic snapshot table has an indexing defect — rows from February and March are incorrectly tagged with January's snapshot_month, causing triple-counting. The fix is to rebuild the snapshot ETL with correct date partitioning.
Account balances should not be stored in a periodic snapshot fact — they are slowly changing attributes and belong in an SCD Type 2 dimension table with an effective_date range.
SUM is the wrong aggregation function — account balances should be aggregated with MAX to return the highest balance across the period, which represents the peak deposit level.
explanation: Account balance is a semi-additive measure: it can be summed across accounts within a single time period (all accounts' January balances sum to total January deposits), but it cannot be summed across time (January + February + March deposits counts each account's money three times). The analyst's query spans 3 months, so every account balance appears 3 times in the result set before SUM runs — producing a value 3× the correct March 31 balance. To get Q1 total deposits, filter to snapshot_month = '2024-03' and SUM across accounts. Option 0 is correct. Option 1 is wrong: a consistent 3× inflation pattern across all accounts is the expected mathematical outcome of summing across 3 monthly snapshots — it is not an ETL or indexing defect. Option 2 is wrong: periodic snapshot is the correct and standard fact table design for account balances — it enables historical trending (balance over time) and point-in-time queries (balance on a specific month-end); SCD Type 2 on a dimension models entity attribute changes, not financial measures. Option 3 is wrong: MAX(balance) returns the highest single account balance across the period, not the total deposits; it is the wrong metric and the wrong aggregation for this use case.
hints: A periodic snapshot fact table stores one balance row per account per month-end. When you include three months in the filter, how many rows does each account contribute to the SUM before the aggregation runs?

Account balance is additive across accounts (all accounts' balances for one month can be summed to get total deposits) but not additive across time periods. Which dimension can it be aggregated across, and which cannot?

title: Determine when a Data Vault hub satellite should be split into two separate satellites
description: A Data Vault customer hub currently has a single satellite (sat_customer) with 40 attributes sourced from both the CRM (25 attributes) and the ERP (15 attributes). After 12 months, the team finds that CRM attributes change 20× more frequently than ERP attributes, and every CRM update produces a full new satellite row including all 15 unchanged ERP columns. Under which principle should the team split this satellite, and into what?
options: Split when the satellite exceeds 30 columns — column count is the primary driver of satellite decomposition in Data Vault.

Split by source system: create sat_customer_crm (25 CRM attributes) and sat_customer_erp (15 ERP attributes). High-churn CRM rows no longer replicate unchanged ERP columns, and each satellite's load timestamp accurately reflects changes from its own source.

Split by change frequency: create sat_customer_volatile (frequently-changing attributes from any source) and sat_customer_stable (infrequently-changing attributes from any source), regardless of which system they come from.
Satellites should never be split per Data Vault standards — one satellite per hub per source system is the canonical rule; splitting violates hub-to-satellite atomicity.
explanation: Data Vault 2.0 satellite design principles include splitting by source system AND by rate of change when they differ. In this case, source alignment and change frequency align: CRM attributes come from one system and change frequently; ERP attributes come from another and change rarely. Splitting into sat_customer_crm and sat_customer_erp means a CRM update creates a new CRM satellite row without touching the ERP satellite — reducing write amplification by 37.5% (15 fewer columns per CRM-sourced row) and keeping each satellite's load_date accurate to its source. Option 1 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: column count is not a splitting criterion in Data Vault; 40 columns is within normal satellite size; the standard splits on source system or change rate, not column count. Option 2 describes a valid alternative split (by change rate across systems), but it mixes source systems in each satellite — a CRM column that happens to be stable sits in the same satellite as an ERP column that is also stable; this makes source-level lineage harder to trace and violates the source-system-per-satellite principle that Data Vault uses for provenance. Option 3 is wrong: Data Vault explicitly permits and encourages satellite splits when source systems or change rates differ — the one-satellite-per-hub constraint applies per-source, not globally; splitting by source is a standard pattern.
hints: Every time a CRM attribute changes, a new satellite row is inserted with all 40 attributes — including 15 ERP columns that did not change. What does this mean for the load_date on ERP attributes, and how accurately does it reflect when ERP data actually changed?

Data Vault satellites are designed to be split by source system (for provenance) or by rate of change (for write efficiency). In this scenario, do source system alignment and change frequency point toward the same split?

title: Identify when denormalization creates reporting correctness problems beyond maintenance cost
description: A data team inlines the customer's region attribute directly into fact_orders as a column (denormalized from dim_customer), eliminating the dimension join for most BI queries. A customer moves from the West region to the East region on October 1. What is the correctness risk introduced by this denormalization, and under what ETL update strategy does it materialize?
options: Denormalization never creates correctness problems in fact tables — region is a slowly changing attribute and the risk is only one of maintenance overhead when it changes.

If the ETL updates the inlined region column on existing fact rows when a customer's region changes, historical orders placed before October 1 will show East region instead of West — the fact table loses its point-in-time accuracy for all pre-change orders.
Denormalization creates a correctness problem only when the fact table has more than 100 columns — below this threshold, the query planner maintains semantic correctness automatically.
The correctness problem manifests only when two customers in different regions share the same customer_id — an edge case that proper deduplication in the dimension prevents.
explanation: When a customer attribute is inlined on the fact row and the ETL performs an UPDATE on existing fact rows when that attribute changes, historical facts lose their point-in-time accuracy — a January order now shows East region even though the customer was in West at the time of purchase. This is not a maintenance cost; it is a semantic correctness error: regional revenue reports for Q1 will silently misattribute transactions. The ETL strategy (overwrite vs. leave-as-is vs. insert-new-fact-row) determines whether this error occurs. Option 1 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: the maintenance cost framing misses the correctness dimension — the issue depends on how the ETL handles updates to inlined attributes; if the ETL overwrites historical fact rows (the most common 'easy' ETL approach), the data is incorrect for historical analysis. Option 2 is wrong: the column count of the fact table is irrelevant to the correctness risk; the risk depends entirely on whether the ETL updates existing rows or preserves the value at insert time. Option 3 is wrong: customer_id uniqueness is not the relevant constraint here; the issue is that any single customer moving regions triggers a potential overwrite of all their historical fact rows if the ETL is not carefully designed to leave historical values intact.
hints: A fact table inlines the customer's region as a column. On October 1, the customer moves from West to East. If the ETL updates this column on all existing fact rows for that customer, what region do historical January orders now show?

A normalized design joins to a dimension at query time — the dimension holds current region, and the fact holds only a key. A denormalized design stores the region inline. Which approach preserves what the region was at the time of the order without any special ETL logic?

title: Design a fractional-credit attribution fact for multi-touchpoint marketing attribution
scenario_context: A marketing attribution team wants to credit the revenue from each closed deal across the 3–7 marketing touchpoints that influenced it (email opens, ad clicks, webinar attendance, sales calls). Each touchpoint receives a fractional credit (e.g., first touch 40%, last touch 40%, middle touches split 20%). The existing fact_deal table has one row per deal with no touchpoint information. dim_touchpoint has one row per touchpoint type.
description: What fact table design correctly models fractional attribution without double-counting total deal revenue at the deal level?
options: Add 7 columns to fact_deal (touchpoint_1_id through touchpoint_7_id with credit_fraction_1 through credit_fraction_7) — this keeps one row per deal while storing all touchpoints.

Create fact_deal_attribution at touchpoint-level grain — one row per (deal_id, touchpoint_id) pair — with a credit_fraction column; total attributed revenue per touchpoint = deal_revenue × credit_fraction, and SUM(credit_fraction) per deal_id = 1.0.
Store a JSON array of touchpoint credits on fact_deal — each element contains touchpoint_id and credit_fraction; the BI tool unpacks the array at query time.

Build a bridge table deal_touchpoint_bridge between fact_deal and dim_touchpoint with a credit_fraction weight column, and compute attributed revenue at query time as deal_revenue × credit_fraction in the SELECT.
explanation: An attribution fact at touchpoint grain is the canonical design: each row carries deal_id, touchpoint_id, credit_fraction, and credited_revenue = deal_revenue × credit_fraction. Because SUM(credit_fraction) per deal = 1.0, summing credited_revenue across all touchpoints for a deal returns the full deal revenue exactly once — no double-counting. Touchpoint-level aggregation (SUM(credited_revenue) GROUP BY touchpoint_type) shows attributed revenue by channel. Option 1 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: 7 sparse columns for up to 7 touchpoints is fragile — deals with 3 touchpoints waste 4 columns; a deal with 8 touchpoints cannot be modeled; and any column-by-column analysis requires pivoting across all 7 columns, making touchpoint-type aggregation complex. Option 2 is wrong: JSON arrays in analytical fact tables defeat column-level filtering, indexing, and aggregation — every query must unpack the array with string parsing functions, which is slow, non-portable, and invisible to schema documentation; JSON is appropriate for semi-structured source landing, not governed analytical facts. Option 3 is partially valid — a bridge table with credit_fraction is a documented Kimball technique — but placing the weight on the bridge rather than on a dedicated attribution fact table means the credited_revenue is never stored as a pre-computable column; complex multi-step JOIN + multiplication must happen in every query, and the bridge pattern is harder to document and test than an explicit attribution fact row.
hints: If each deal has 3–7 touchpoints and credit_fraction must sum to 1.0 per deal, how many rows does the attribution model need per deal — and which table type is designed to store one row per event or allocation unit?

If attributed revenue per row = deal_revenue × credit_fraction, and SUM(credit_fraction) per deal = 1.0, what does SUM(attributed_revenue) across all rows for one deal return — and is that the right answer?

title: Evaluate the GDPR data minimization constraint on a historically versioned customer dimension
description: A company uses a versioned dimension design to track customer tier history — each tier change creates a new row alongside the previous rows, indefinitely retained. GDPR's data minimization principle requires that personal data not be kept longer than necessary for its stated purpose. The legal team asks whether historical tier-change rows containing personal identifiers (name, email, customer_id) constitute personal data requiring a retention limit. What is the data team's correct response?
options: Historical dimension rows do not contain personal data — only current-state dimension rows are personal data under GDPR; historical versions are analytical records exempt from minimization.

Historical dimension rows that contain personal identifiers (name, email, customer_id) are personal data under GDPR regardless of whether they are 'old' versions — the data team should implement a retention policy that either deletes or pseudonymizes identifiers on dimension rows older than the agreed retention window, while preserving the tier-change structure for analytics.
GDPR data minimization does not apply to data warehouses — it applies only to operational systems that interact directly with customers; analytical systems are exempt by design.
The only compliant solution is to delete all historical dimension rows and switch to SCD Type 1 — GDPR minimization cannot be satisfied while retaining any historical customer rows.
explanation: GDPR's definition of personal data includes any information that directly or indirectly identifies a natural person — historical dimension rows carrying name, email, or customer_id are personal data regardless of their 'version' status. The data minimization principle requires that data be kept only as long as necessary for its purpose. The correct response is to implement a retention policy: rows older than the retention window have their direct identifiers replaced with pseudonyms or nulled out (tombstone pattern), while the tier-change structure (tier_value, effective_from, effective_to, a pseudonymous key) is preserved for analytical integrity. Option 1 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: the GDPR does not exempt historical versions of personal data — 'old row' is not a legal category; if a row contains a field that identifies a person, it is personal data. Option 2 is wrong: GDPR applies to any system that processes personal data of EU residents, including data warehouses; there is no analytical system exemption, and major DPA enforcement actions have explicitly included data warehouse and analytics platform data. Option 3 is wrong: switching to overwrite (Type 1) would satisfy minimization by removing history but destroys the business value (historical reporting, regulatory audit trails of tier changes) the warehouse was built to provide; pseudonymization after a retention window achieves compliance without destroying analytical value.
hints: Historical tier-change rows in a versioned dimension contain the customer's name, email, and identifier alongside each old tier value. Does GDPR's definition of personal data apply to a row because it is 'historical' or because it contains an identifying field?

A tombstone approach nulls out personal identifiers (name, email) after a retention window but keeps the tier and date columns. Does this satisfy GDPR data minimization while preserving the historical tier-change structure for analytics?

title: Govern source system precedence when two marts define the same dimension attribute with conflicting values
scenario_context: Two business units produce conflicting values for customer acquisition_channel: Marketing uses Salesforce (CRM) as the source of truth, where acquisition_channel reflects the first touchpoint. Finance uses the ERP, where acquisition_channel reflects the payment method used at first purchase. Both teams reference the same customer IDs. When a conformed customer dimension is built, the data team must pick one source for acquisition_channel — or handle both — for a shared executive dashboard.
description: What governance process and modeling approach should the data team use to resolve this conflict correctly?
options: Default to the ERP value — financial systems are always the authoritative system of record for customer data across the enterprise.

Store both values in the conformed dimension (crm_acquisition_channel and erp_acquisition_channel), document the business definition of each, and surface both to the executive dashboard so stakeholders can decide which to use for each report.

Convene a cross-functional governance session with Marketing, Finance, and the executive dashboard owner to align on a single canonical definition; encode the agreed definition in the conformed dimension and document the decision with a lineage note. If business units legitimately need different definitions, name them explicitly and maintain both as governed variants.
Use whichever source system has more complete data for acquisition_channel — coverage percentage is the objective tiebreaker for conflicting source systems.
explanation: Conformed dimension governance requires business agreement before technical implementation. The conflict is semantic, not technical: Marketing and Finance use the same label ('acquisition_channel') for conceptually different things (first touchpoint vs. payment method). A cross-functional governance process names the disagreement, aligns on definitions, and either selects one canonical value or legitimizes both as distinct named attributes (first_touchpoint_channel, payment_channel). The technical implementation follows the business decision. Option 2 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: 'financial systems are always authoritative' is an organizational policy, not a universal fact — the ERP's acquisition_channel (payment method) is not obviously more correct than the CRM's (first marketing touchpoint) for a marketing attribution dashboard; authority must be established per attribute, not per system. Option 1 is wrong: exposing both values without a governance decision replicates the confusion at the dashboard level — executives will ask 'which one do I use?' and receive no authoritative answer, perpetuating the same conflict in reporting that prompted the question. Option 3 is wrong: coverage percentage answers 'which source has fewer NULLs' but not 'which source's definition is the right one for the agreed analytical purpose'; a source with 99% coverage of the wrong definition is worse than a 70% coverage source with the right definition.
hints: When two source systems define acquisition_channel differently — first marketing touchpoint in one, payment method at purchase in another — can a single shared dimension table contain one acquisition_channel value that is semantically correct for both Finance's and Marketing's reports simultaneously?

If the data team picks Salesforce without asking Finance, and Finance later discovers the executive dashboard uses the CRM definition for a metric they own, what happens to trust in the conformed dimension?

title: Resolve conflicting 'active user' metric definitions across three teams before an IPO filing
scenario_context: Three teams have each defined 'Monthly Active Users' differently in the semantic layer: Product defines it as users who triggered any event in 30 days; Growth defines it as users who completed a core action (purchase or booking) in 30 days; Finance defines it as unique users with any session lasting more than 5 minutes. The CFO must report a single MAU figure in SEC filings. All three definitions produce materially different numbers.
description: What is the correct process and technical implementation to produce a single, defensible MAU definition for regulatory reporting?
options: Use the highest of the three numbers — regulators expect companies to report the most favorable metric, and the Product definition is the most inclusive.
Use the lowest of the three numbers — conservative metrics reduce legal exposure; the Growth definition (core actions) is most defensible as it reflects genuine engagement.

Convene a governance process with Legal, Finance, and Product to agree on a single canonical MAU definition backed by a business rationale; encode that definition in the semantic layer as the official 'mau' metric, rename the others with explicit qualifiers (mau_any_event, mau_core_action, mau_session_5min), and document the rationale in the metric's metadata.
Expose all three definitions in the SEC filing with footnotes explaining each — transparency about metric methodology satisfies regulatory requirements better than picking one.
explanation: Regulatory filings require a consistent, documented, and business-rationale-backed metric definition — not the most favorable or most conservative number, but the most defensible one agreed upon by the business and legal teams. The semantic layer then enforces the canonical definition technically. Renaming the other definitions to explicit qualifiers (rather than deleting them) preserves analytical utility while ensuring there is no confusion about which MAU is the 'official' one. Option 2 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: selecting the highest metric to look favorable is exactly the kind of metric inflation that attracts SEC scrutiny — MAU manipulation was central to several high-profile enforcement actions; the choice must be anchored in business rationale. Option 1 is wrong: conservative is not the same as correct — the right metric is defined by what the company's business model identifies as meaningful engagement, not by which number is smallest; choosing arbitrarily for legal safety without a rationale is itself a governance failure. Option 3 is wrong: footnoting multiple definitions without picking one is not how SEC MAU reporting works — the SEC expects a primary metric with a clear definition; multiple competing definitions in a single filing invite enforcement questions about which figure management actually relies on.
hints: When three teams each have a different definition of 'active user' in the semantic layer, can an executive report reference all three simultaneously as 'the company's active user count' in an SEC filing?
The semantic layer can enforce whichever definition is agreed upon — but who makes the decision about which definition is canonical, and what makes that decision defensible to a regulator?

title: Diagnose revenue fan-out from a multi-valued pricing-tier dimension joined directly to a sales fact
scenario_context: A revenue operations report shows total revenue inflating by a consistent factor of ~3.5× per product. The query joins fact_sales (one row per order line) to dim_product (one row per product) and then to dim_product_pricing_tier, which has one row per product per active pricing tier — products have 2–5 active tiers simultaneously (volume discount tiers, channel-specific tiers, promotional tiers). The analyst includes a filter on a single tier_type but applies it with OR across all three tier_type values, inadvertently un-filtering the join.
description: What is the structural root cause and the correct resolution strategy?
options: The filter's OR logic is the only problem — changing it to AND would eliminate the fan-out without any schema change.

The many-to-many relationship between products and pricing tiers is not modeled with a bridge table; joining fact_sales to dim_product_pricing_tier on product_id fans out the fact row to all matching tier rows (averaging 3.5 per product), replicating revenue before aggregation. The fix is either a bridge table with explicit allocation logic or a query-rewrite that pre-filters to one tier per product before joining.
The root cause is that dim_product_pricing_tier is missing a primary key constraint — duplicate tier rows inflate the join result.
Pricing tiers should not be stored in a dimension at all — they are a fact-level attribute and should be columns on fact_sales instead.
explanation: A direct JOIN from fact_sales to dim_product_pricing_tier on product_id is a many-to-many join: each order line fans out to all matching tier rows for that product. With an average of 3.5 tiers per product, every revenue value is replicated 3.5 times before SUM aggregates — producing the observed inflation. The OR filter compounds this but is not the root cause; even a correctly written AND filter would still fan out revenue if multiple tiers matched. The structural fix is to determine the analytic intent: if revenue should be attributed to all tiers simultaneously, a bridge table with credit_fraction solves it; if only the applied tier matters, pre-filter dim_product_pricing_tier to one row per product (the actually-applied tier for each order) before joining. Option 1 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: the OR filter is a secondary issue — fixing it reduces the multiplier from 3.5 to fewer matching tiers, but does not eliminate the structural many-to-many problem; any product with more than 1 tier matching the corrected filter still fans out. Option 2 is wrong: missing primary key constraints produce duplicates at the dimension level, which also fans out, but the 3.5× factor correlates with the average tier count per product (as described), not with arbitrary duplicates — duplicate rows would produce inconsistent multipliers, not a consistent factor. Option 3 is wrong: pricing tiers are a dimension of products (they describe product attributes), not a fact-level measure; moving them to fact_sales would require knowing at order time which tier applied — that information belongs in the order itself, not as a static column on the fact schema.
hints: fact_sales has one row per order line. dim_product_pricing_tier has 2–5 rows per product. When these two tables are joined on product_id without any pre-aggregation, how many rows does the join produce per order line on average?
If the filter was correctly written but a product still has 3 matching tier rows, what does SUM(revenue) return after the join — and is that the correct revenue for that order line?

title: Choose between OBT, Lakehouse medallion, and Kimball star schema for a new analytics platform under specific constraints
scenario_context: A company is designing a new analytics platform from scratch. Constraints: (1) source schemas change 2–3 times per year; (2) data science team needs row-level access to raw events; (3) BI team needs sub-second dashboard queries on pre-aggregated metrics; (4) the platform must support point-in-time audit queries for regulators. The team is choosing between: OBT (all dimensions pre-joined), Lakehouse medallion (bronze/silver/gold), and Kimball star schema.
description: Which architecture, or combination, best satisfies all four constraints?
options: OBT (one big table) — pre-joining all dimensions satisfies the BI team's performance requirement, and the full row-level data satisfies the DS team; schema changes require a single-table migration.
Kimball star schema only — fact and dimension tables satisfy BI requirements; DS team queries the star schema directly; schema changes require coordinated dimension migrations.

Lakehouse medallion (bronze: raw events, silver: cleansed entity-resolved records, gold: pre-aggregated marts) with star schema marts in gold — bronze satisfies DS raw access and audit, silver handles schema change isolation, gold/star satisfies BI performance. The medallion layers complement rather than replace each other.

Data Vault for ingestion, OBT in gold — Data Vault absorbs schema changes at ingestion, and OBT in the gold layer satisfies the BI performance requirement; DS team queries the Data Vault satellite tables directly for raw access.
explanation: The medallion architecture with star schema marts in gold satisfies all four constraints with distinct layers: bronze absorbs raw events (DS access, audit point-in-time replay by filtering to loads before a given date), silver applies schema-change-tolerant cleansing (schema changes at source are handled in the bronze→silver transformation without touching gold), and gold star schema marts deliver the pre-aggregated performance the BI team requires. Each layer is independently queryable. Option 2 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: OBT does not satisfy constraint 4 (point-in-time audit) — a single pre-joined flat table has no bronze-level append-only raw record that can reconstruct what the warehouse knew at any historical date; schema changes also require rebuilding the entire wide table. Option 1 is wrong: a pure Kimball star schema has no bronze/raw layer for the DS team (they would query transformed dimension and fact tables, not raw events), and schema changes at the source propagate directly to the star schema without an isolation layer; point-in-time audit is possible only if the star schema itself is append-only, which is non-standard. Option 3 is partially valid — Data Vault handles schema changes and raw audit — but OBT in the gold layer reintroduces constraint 0's schema volatility problem when the OBT must be rebuilt after Data Vault satellite changes; the DS team querying raw satellite tables requires familiarity with Data Vault's hub-link-satellite structure, which is technically demanding for data scientists focused on model development.
hints: A Lakehouse medallion architecture and a Kimball-style mart layer both produce analytics-ready tables in their gold layer. What does the bronze layer provide that a pre-aggregated mart layer alone cannot — specifically for point-in-time audit queries and raw event access?
When a source schema changes mid-year, which layer of the medallion architecture absorbs the change without requiring the gold star schema to be rebuilt?

title: Design a zero-downtime fact table schema migration when a new business line requires incompatible new dimension attributes
scenario_context: An e-commerce company launches a B2B subscription business line mid-year. The existing fact_order table has columns for: customer_id, product_id, order_date, revenue, promo_id. Subscription orders require three new required dimensions: contract_id, subscription_term_months, and billing_cycle. These attributes are meaningless (NULL) for the original retail orders. The data team must migrate without downtime and without breaking existing BI dashboards.
description: What is the correct zero-downtime schema migration strategy for this scenario?
options: Add contract_id, subscription_term_months, and billing_cycle as nullable columns to fact_order and NULL-fill them for all historical retail orders — existing queries are unaffected since they don't reference the new columns.
Create a separate fact_subscription_order table for the new business line and union it with fact_order in a view that downstream queries can use as a single access point.

Migrate fact_order to a wide OBT format by adding all new subscription columns as NULLable with a business_line discriminator column; update all existing BI queries to add WHERE business_line = 'retail' to restore original results.
Create a new version of the fact table (fact_order_v2) with all new columns, migrate historical data to the new schema, and switch BI queries over a two-week cutover window.
explanation: Adding nullable columns to an existing fact table is the standard zero-downtime additive migration: existing rows get NULL for the new columns, existing queries are unaffected (they do not reference columns they do not know about), and new subscription rows populate the new columns. Dashboards continue to run against the original schema without modification. Option 0 is correct. Option 1 is wrong: two separate fact tables require BI tools to know which table to query based on business line — every query must be redesigned with a UNION or a view layer; this is not zero-downtime from the user perspective, as all existing queries must be migrated to reference the view. Option 2 is wrong: adding a business_line discriminator and updating existing queries defeats the 'zero-downtime' requirement — all BI queries must be modified to add the WHERE clause, which is a coordinated migration requiring downtime of the dashboard development cycle, not just the database. Option 3 is wrong: creating a new table version with a cutover window is the most disruptive approach — it requires migrating historical data (compute-intensive), maintaining two active tables during the window, and updating all BI queries before the cutover date; this is a planned migration, not zero-downtime.
hints: If new columns are added as nullable to an existing fact table, what happens to existing BI queries that don't reference those columns — do they break, slow down, or continue unaffected?
The new subscription columns are meaningless for retail orders. Does NULL in those columns for retail rows create any reporting correctness risk for dashboards that only query retail metrics?

title: Extend a shared customer dimension when a new subsidiary uses an incompatible tier classification system
scenario_context: A parent company (Company A) has used a 4-tier customer classification (Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum) tracked with versioned history for 3 years. A new subsidiary (Company B) is onboarded; Company B uses an 8-level tier system (1–8) based on different lifecycle criteria. Both companies' customers must appear in the shared customer dimension for cross-company reporting. The existing tier_code column is an integer constrained to 1–4.
description: What is the most governance-sound approach to extend the customer dimension for Company B's tier system?
options: Expand tier_code to allow values 1–8 — both companies' customers coexist with a single column; Company A uses codes 1–4 and Company B uses codes 1–8, distinguished by a source_company column.
Add a company_b_tier_code column alongside tier_code; a source_company column disambiguates which tier schema applies per row; existing historical Company A rows are unchanged.

Align both companies on a canonical tier taxonomy (e.g., a 5-level shared classification) through a governance process; map both source tier systems to the canonical codes; expose source-specific tiers as separate attributes for internal use within each subsidiary.
Maintain two separate customer dimension tables (dim_customer_a and dim_customer_b) and join them in the reporting layer using a UNION with a company discriminator.
explanation: A conformed dimension requires that a shared attribute means the same thing across all fact tables that reference it. Allowing two incompatible tier schemas (1–4 vs. 1–8) to coexist in one column or as two separate columns without a canonical mapping makes cross-company tier analysis impossible — 'Tier 3' means different things for Company A and Company B. A governance process that maps both source systems to a shared canonical taxonomy enables unified reporting (e.g., 'combined customers at Platinum-equivalent tier') while preserving source-level detail as separate attributes for subsidiary-specific analysis. Option 2 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: allowing Company B to use codes 1–8 in the same tier_code column used by Company A means tier_code 3 is ambiguous (it means Gold for Company A and an intermediate Company B tier) — cross-company queries are semantically incorrect even with a source_company filter. Option 1 is wrong: two parallel tier columns without a canonical mapping leaves the cross-company tier comparison problem unsolved — the executive dashboard still has no single 'equivalent tier' to filter on; it only shifts the ambiguity from one column to two columns. Option 3 is wrong: UNION joins in the reporting layer with a company discriminator produce a combined list of customers but no unified tier concept — a filter on tier still requires two separate WHERE clauses with different tier semantics, and the query planner cannot use a shared index; this is the reporting-layer workaround that conformed dimensions are specifically designed to replace.
hints: A shared customer dimension has a tier_code column that means Gold/Platinum for Company A and a completely different lifecycle level for Company B. Can a cross-company dashboard filter on tier_code = 3 and get a meaningful result that applies to both companies?

Canonical mapping — translating both source tier systems to a shared taxonomy — requires a governance decision about equivalence. What does the canonical mapping enable that simply adding a Company B column does not?

title: Distinguish semantic layer metrics from dbt mart metrics and identify when each fails
description: A company's semantic layer defines a metric 'revenue' that filters to closed-won opportunities only. A dbt mart also has a column named 'revenue' that includes deals with probability > 80% (pipeline revenue). Both are exposed to BI users. The CFO queries 'revenue' in the dashboard and gets $50 M; a data analyst queries the mart directly and gets $75 M. Neither the CFO nor the analyst knows they are looking at different definitions. Under what governance failure did this occur, and when does each approach specifically fail to protect against it?
options: The semantic layer fails because it applies a filter the user did not request — the mart's broader definition is more appropriate for a default revenue metric.
The dbt mart fails because mart column names should never be exposed directly to end users — all BI access must route through the semantic layer to prevent definition drift.

Both approaches fail when metric naming is not governed: the semantic layer fails to protect BI users if mart tables are also directly queryable under the same metric name; the mart column fails to communicate its definition when exposed without documentation. The fix is a naming convention (e.g., revenue_closed_won vs. revenue_pipeline), enforced access routing to the semantic layer for BI tools, and mart column documentation.

Neither approach fails — the discrepancy is a data freshness issue; the semantic layer refreshes daily while the mart refreshes hourly, producing a $25 M difference from new deals closed during the day.
explanation: The semantic layer's value proposition is a single canonical definition — but it fails if BI users can bypass it and query mart tables directly under similar column names. The mart's value proposition is a governed, documented column — but it fails if it is undocumented and shares a name with the semantic layer's differently-defined metric. Both failures are governance failures, not technical ones: the semantic layer's definition is not the source of truth if mart access is uncontrolled, and the mart's column is not governed if it has no documentation and no naming discipline. Option 2 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: the semantic layer's filter is not arbitrary — it encodes a business decision about what 'revenue' means for executive reporting; the broader mart definition may be valid for pipeline analysis but not for the CFO's closed-business metric. Option 1 is wrong: routing all BI access through the semantic layer is a valid enforcement approach but does not address the naming collision — if a user ever queries the mart directly (e.g., a data scientist), they encounter the same ambiguity; naming discipline is required regardless of routing. Option 3 is wrong: a $25 M gap between closed-won and pipeline-inclusive definitions is a semantic difference, not a staleness difference; closed-won deals do not appear in pipeline revenue, so no amount of freshness synchronization would close the definitional gap.
hints: A semantic layer metric named 'revenue' and a mart column also named 'revenue' both exist and produce different numbers. If a BI user can reach both, what prevents them from accidentally using the wrong definition?

The semantic layer enforces its definition for queries routed through it. What happens to its governance value when analysts query mart tables directly using SQL clients — and what naming or access control fixes this?

title: Identify when an OBT's inlined dimension attributes produce correct-looking but semantically wrong aggregation results
description: A team builds an OBT by inlining the customer's region attribute onto every order row at the time the order is loaded. Customer region changes over time (relocation). An analyst queries 'total revenue by region for last quarter' and the result looks plausible but is consistently 8% higher in the East region and 6% lower in the West compared to the benchmark report. Under what specific OBT loading strategy does this correctness error occur?
options: The error occurs when the OBT loading strategy overwrites the inlined region column on all existing order rows whenever a customer's region changes — historical orders are re-attributed to the customer's new region, silently transferring revenue across regions.
The error occurs because OBTs always inflate East region revenue due to the higher average order value of East-region customers being applied retroactively to all historical rows.
The error occurs only when the OBT is partitioned by region — re-partitioning after a region change moves rows between partitions and corrupts the row count.
The error occurs because the analyst's query is filtering on the wrong date column — the OBT's load_date rather than the order_date causes region attribution to shift for recently loaded rows.
explanation: When the OBT ETL updates the inlined region column on all historical order rows whenever a customer relocates, those historical orders are now attributed to the new region — revenue that occurred while the customer was in West now shows under East. This is semantically incorrect for any point-in-time analysis. A normalized design avoids this by joining to the dimension at query time, where the analyst can choose current-region attribution or point-in-time attribution by selecting the appropriate dimension row version. Option 0 is correct. Option 1 is wrong: 'East region has higher AOV' is a dataset property, not a structural OBT flaw; OBTs do not systematically inflate any specific region — the error pattern depends on the relocation direction and ETL strategy, not geography. Option 2 is wrong: re-partitioning moves rows between storage partitions for performance, which changes query performance but does not change the data values or the region column's value on any row — partition-key updates affect WHERE clause pruning, not data correctness. Option 3 is wrong: load_date vs. order_date filtering is a common query error but would produce a date-range discrepancy, not a consistent regional attribution shift — the 8%/6% regional split is diagnostic of cross-regional re-attribution, not a date filter issue.
hints: An OBT table stores region inline on every order row at load time. A customer moves from West to East on November 1. If the ETL runs an UPDATE to set region = 'East' on all that customer's historical rows, what region do their January orders now show?

In a normalized design, a query joins to the customer dimension and can choose which version of the dimension to use (current vs. historical). What flexibility does the OBT's inlined column lose when it is overwritten on region change?

title: Evaluate when normalizing attributes within a Data Vault satellite provides architectural value
description: A hub's satellite stores three customer attributes from the same CRM: email, region, and account_tier. These three attributes change at very different rates: email changes once per year on average, region changes quarterly, and account_tier changes monthly. A senior engineer proposes normalizing within the satellite by splitting it into three separate satellites, one per attribute. Under what condition does this intra-satellite normalization provide tangible analytical or operational value?
options: When the satellite exceeds 20 columns — intra-attribute normalization is only beneficial beyond this threshold; 3-column satellites should always remain together.

When the attributes have significantly different change rates: one satellite per attribute means a monthly tier change inserts only a new tier row (1 column) instead of replicating the stable email and region alongside it — reducing write amplification and ensuring each attribute's load_date accurately reflects only that attribute's change, not coincidental changes to other attributes.

When the CRM source system enforces separate change-tracking on each attribute — intra-satellite normalization mirrors the source system's internal event model and is only appropriate when the source itself treats each attribute as an independent record.

Intra-satellite normalization is never appropriate — the satellite design principle in Data Vault is one satellite per source system per hub, and splitting by attribute violates the source-atomicity contract.
explanation: When attributes on the same satellite change at very different rates, a single satellite conflates their histories: a monthly tier change inserts a new row with the current email and region as well — even though those didn't change — and their load_date updates to the tier-change date. This makes it appear that email and region changed monthly alongside tier, obscuring their true change history. Splitting into one satellite per attribute (or per rate-of-change group) means each satellite's load_date accurately reflects its own attribute's change history, and write amplification for high-churn attributes decreases. Option 1 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: column count is not the driver for intra-satellite splitting in Data Vault 2.0; the driver is change rate (and source system, which is already a first-level split). Option 2 is wrong: Data Vault satellite design does not require that the source system itself tracks each attribute as an independent event — the modeling decision is an architectural choice in the warehouse, not a mirror of source system internals; warehouses regularly split on change rate regardless of source event structure. Option 3 is wrong: Data Vault 2.0 explicitly permits and recommends splitting satellites by rate of change as an optimization; the one-satellite-per-source-per-hub rule is a minimum, not a maximum — further splits by change rate are documented standard practice.
hints: A satellite stores email, region, and tier on the same row. When tier changes monthly, a new satellite row is inserted — but the load_date on the new row now also reflects when email and region 'changed,' even though they didn't. What does this do to the accuracy of email and region change history?

If email is in its own satellite and only changes once per year, how many rows does the email satellite accumulate over 3 years compared to a combined satellite that re-inserts email alongside every monthly tier change?

title: Debug a cross-fact double-count when two fact tables at different levels of detail share a customer dimension
scenario_context: A query joins fact_order (one row per order), fact_return (one row per returned item, multiple per order), and dim_customer (one row per customer) in a single SELECT to compute net revenue = SUM(order_revenue) - SUM(return_amount) per customer segment. The result shows net revenue approximately 4× higher than the GL balance. Investigation shows orders have an average of 3.8 returned items when a return occurs.
description: What is the structural cause of the inflation, and how should the query be restructured?
options: fact_return is missing rows — the 4× inflation indicates that some return amounts are negative and their absolute values are being summed instead of subtracted.

Joining both facts to dim_customer in the same query creates a three-way join where each order row fans out to all matching return rows for that customer, replicating order_revenue once per return row; net revenue must be computed by aggregating each fact to the customer segment level independently, then joining the two aggregates.
The customer dimension has duplicate rows for customers with multiple addresses — the join to dim_customer causes the double-count regardless of the return fact.

SUM(order_revenue) - SUM(return_amount) is algebraically incorrect for net revenue — the correct formula is SUM(order_revenue - return_amount) computed on a row-by-row basis within the same fact table.
explanation: When fact_order and fact_return are joined to the same dim_customer in one query, the join engine must reconcile two different granularities through a shared key. If the JOIN path is dim_customer → fact_order → fact_return (or the equivalent), each order row joins to all return rows for that customer — producing an order × return Cartesian product per customer. With 3.8 return items per order on average, order_revenue is replicated 3.8 times in the join result before SUM runs. The correct approach is to compute each fact's customer-segment total independently (one CTE per fact, both grouped to customer_segment) and then join the two aggregated results — never joining raw mismatched-level facts through a shared dimension in a single SELECT. Option 1 is correct. Option 0 is wrong: missing return rows or negative values would reduce the return SUM, making net revenue too high by a small amount from undercounting returns — not a 4× inflation; negative sign handling would cause subtraction to become addition but would produce erratic results, not a consistent 4× factor. Option 2 is wrong: a customer dimension with duplicate rows for multiple addresses would fan out every order and return row equally, producing a consistent multiplier based on address count — but dim_customer typically has one row per customer (addresses may be handled separately); this would not produce a 3.8× factor. Option 3 is wrong: the formula SUM(order_revenue) - SUM(return_amount) is algebraically equivalent to SUM(order_revenue - return_amount) when the rows are correctly aligned at the same granularity — the issue here is not the formula but that the rows are NOT aligned (facts are at different granularities).
hints: A query joins fact_order (one row per order) and fact_return (one row per returned item, multiple per order) through the same dim_customer. If a customer has 1 order and 4 return items, how many rows does the three-way join produce for that customer?
If each order row fans out to 4 return rows during the join, how many times does order_revenue appear in the result set before SUM aggregates — and what does this do to the total?

title: Debug a monthly p95 latency undercount caused by averaging pre-computed weekly percentiles
scenario_context: A platform team stores pre-computed p95_latency_ms (95th percentile of request latency) per week in an aggregate table. An SRE analyst computes monthly p95 by averaging the four weekly p95 values: (p95_week1 + p95_week2 + p95_week3 + p95_week4) / 4. The result is consistently 30–40% lower than the true monthly p95 computed directly from the raw event log. The discrepancy is largest in weeks with traffic spikes.
description: What is the structural cause of the undercount, and what is the correct approach to compute monthly p95 from a weekly aggregate table?
options: The weekly p95 values are computed over too small a sample — 95th percentile estimates are unreliable for weekly windows with fewer than 1 000 requests; the fix is to widen the window to monthly from the start.

Averaging four weekly p95 values applies equal weight to each week regardless of request volume; a high-traffic week (e.g., 500 000 requests) contributes the same weight as a low-traffic week (e.g., 10 000 requests), making the arithmetic mean systematically lower than the true p95 over all requests in the month.
The pre-computed p95 values are stored as integers (milliseconds rounded to the nearest integer) — rounding error compounds across four weeks, producing a 30–40% undercount.
The SRE analyst should use MAX(p95_week1, p95_week2, p95_week3, p95_week4) instead of the arithmetic average — the maximum weekly p95 is the correct conservative estimate for monthly p95.
explanation: Percentiles are non-additive and cannot be re-aggregated by averaging. The 95th percentile of the combined monthly distribution is determined by the distribution of all requests — a week with 500 000 requests dominates the monthly percentile calculation far more than a week with 10 000 requests. The arithmetic average of weekly p95 values gives each week equal weight, effectively assuming equal traffic volumes across all weeks. During traffic spikes, the spike week's p95 (which is higher than normal) is diluted by the three normal weeks in the average, producing a monthly p95 that is lower than the true value. Option 1 is correct. The fix requires either storing per-request latency in the aggregate table (not feasible at scale) or storing request counts alongside each weekly p95 and applying a weighted approximation — but true p95 re-aggregation is mathematically impossible from only weekly p95 values; the data team must compute p95 directly from the raw event log for monthly periods. Option 0 is wrong: p95 estimates are statistically reliable for samples of 1 000+ requests; the systematic 30–40% undercount is not a sample-size problem but an algebraic re-aggregation error. Option 2 is wrong: integer rounding at the millisecond level (even 500 ms rounding) would produce errors far smaller than 30–40% — rounding cannot explain that magnitude of systematic bias. Option 3 is wrong: MAX(weekly p95) is the most conservative approach and avoids the undercount, but it is not the true monthly p95 — it is the worst weekly p95, which overstates the true monthly value in most cases and is not a statistically meaningful metric.
hints: p95 latency is a percentile — the latency value below which 95% of requests fall in a given window. If Week 1 has 500 000 requests with p95 = 800 ms and Week 2 has 10 000 requests with p95 = 200 ms, does arithmetic average correctly represent the monthly p95 over 510 000 total requests?

Pre-computed summary statistics like percentiles cannot be re-aggregated by simple arithmetic — unlike revenue (which can be summed) or counts (which can be summed). What information is lost when a weekly p95 is stored without its underlying request count?
